#9211. The ‘Enough’ Is for All You Small Phone Fans

The ‘Enough’ Is for All You Small Phone Fans

Not everyone is stoked that smartphones keep getting larger, offering ever-bigger displays. In fact, some people are very much in love with the small phones of years past. New smartphone company Enough believes there are, well, enough of those people to justify launching an all-new small smartphone in 2026.

As The Verge‘s Alison Johnson remarks, it may seem like a risky time to make a new smartphone. Flash storage and chip prices are through the roof. Inflation is tightening people’s pursestrings. But maybe these same factors make it a good time to launch a smaller, relatively cheaper phone that doesn’t skimp on all the modern amenities that people expect from their jumbo, erm, regular, smartphones.

“In a sea of 6″ + slabs, enough stands small at 5.3″,” the company explains.

For reference, the base iPhone 17 smartphone has a 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR display. Those who want an iPhone with a much smaller screen must hit the used market, seeking out something like an iPhone 13 mini with its 5.4-inch screen. It’s much the same story on the Android side of things, where perhaps average phones are actually even bigger.

The Enough, which has raised nearly $130,500 of its $250,000 goal on Kickstarter so far with 28 days left in the campaign, harkens back to a bygone era of relatively small smartphones.

However, unlike most modern phones that have made screens bigger while simultaneously making chassises thinner and thinner, the Enough phone doesn’t worry much about being slim. It’s 12 millimeters (0.47 inches) thick, making it a relatively chonky fella. It’s thicker than the new folding iPhone Duo is when it’s closed. Actually, the iPhone Duo is an interesting comparison because its outer display is 5.4 inches diagonally. While the Enough is relatively taller, they aren’t that different in terms of size.

They are a lot different in terms of functionality and price, though. Enough starts at $449 for early bird backers and will retail for $599 after the Kickstarter campaign closes, supposing it goes well for the brand, that is.

Enough also differs from modern smartphone makers in its approach to repairability. Part of the reason why it’s a relatively thick phone is that it has a user-removable and replaceable 3,500mAh battery, a true rarity in today’s market.

On the inside, the phone has a MediaTek Dimensity 7500 processor, 8GB of RAM, and 128GB of storage (with expandable storage). It runs Android 17 and OdysseyOS. It features 5G wireless, Wi-Fi 6 (2.4+5GHz), GPS, Bluetooth, NFC, a fingerprint sensor, and Face ID. It has a physical SIM slot and supports eSIM.

As for cameras, this is where mobile photographers may scoff a bit. There’s but one rear camera, a 50-megapixel Sony IMX766 module. Enough doesn’t say anything about the lens, but the IMX766 is a relatively normal Type 1/1.56 image sensor. A 24mm or 25mm equivalent lens should be expected, with the ability to crop in a bit for 2x or maybe 4x digital zoom. There’s also a front-facing 32-megapixel camera. Enough doesn’t specify video recording, but the sensor itself supports 4Kp24.

As of right now, Enough intends to ship to backers in May 2027. As mentioned, early bird backing starts at $449 and the retail price is expected to be $599.

#9208. DaVinci Resolve Now Supports Apple’s Brand-New Touchscreen Mac

DaVinci Resolve Now Supports Apple’s Brand-New Touchscreen Mac

Apple’s brand-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, the first Mac to ever feature a touchscreen, arrives today, and Blackmagic Design’s DaVinci Resolve 21 video editor is ready.

DaVinci Resolve 21.2 introduces many updates, fixes, and improvements, including full compatibility and support for the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR touchscreen. PetaPixel‘s Jaron Schneider reviewed the new MacBook Pro, awarding it a 10 and, of course, Editor’s Choice.

However, while the big highlight is the touchscreen, it is the fundamentally new Tandem OLED screen technology that truly impresses. Whether users touch it or not, it’s the best display ever in a laptop, absolutely smashing PetaPixel‘s display benchmark tests and delivering truly absurd color performance and consistency.

“This is a remarkable display,” Schneider writes, emphasis his. Between that beautiful display and the MacBook Pro’s class-leading performance in DaVinci Resolve, video editors should be beside themselves, whether they ever use touch inside DaVinci Resolve or not. But now, at least, they can.

The update also adds support for Blackmagic Design Gen 6 LUTs, workflow improvements for audio and multicam clips, support for EXIF data in PNG files, and a bunch of bug fixes. The full list of changes is available on Blackmagic’s support center, and DaVinci Resolve 21.2 is available now as a free update for all Resolve 21 users, including free users and those with the paid Studio version.

The Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks are a notable update. This new color science arrived in September inside Blackmagic RAW 6.0, the company’s professional RAW codec. While Blackmagic’s own cameras utilize Blackmagic RAW (BRAW), some third-party cameras do as well via external recording, including Sony FX-series cameras. Blackmagic says BRAW is the “world’s fastest RAW format,” and now it’s even better and fully supported inside DaVinci Resolve.

Speaking of purchasing DaVinci Resolve 21, Blackmagic Design announced a limited-time special on its flagship video editing app a few weeks ago. DaVinci Resolve 21 Studio is currently 20% off through November 20, so video editors still have two weeks to take advantage of the deal. With the discount, DaVinci Resolve 21 (21.2 now) drops from $295 to $236.

By the way, the company’s own portable DaVinci Resolve Speed Editor, which comes with DaVinci Resolve Studio, is also 20% off right now. That knocks it down from $435 to $348, meaning that customers are basically getting the dedicated controller unit for $112.

#9206. Dezeen's favourite furniture and homeware from October

The first piece of furniture by architecture office Studio Hagen Hall and a pleated cabinet by Didi Ng Wing Yin feature in this roundup of design pieces spotted by Dezeen’s Jane Englefield over the last month.

Louis Hagen Hall of London-based Studio Hagen Hall has made his first foray into furniture with this sculptural coffee table, delivered as two legs and a weighty glass tabletop that require no mechanical fixings.

Hagen Hall originally designed the asymmetric piece for Pine Heath, a modernist Hampstead renovation with a corner sofa that required a bespoke coffee table to offset the negative space left by the seating.

Cherry veneer legs are paired with recyclable brown smoked glass to create the made-to-order piece, informed by the design philosophy of modernist American architect John Lautner.

Austrian, Netherlands-based designer Flora Lechner originally caught the attention of London’s Max Radford Gallery with her alternative aluminium chandeliers that look like ornate robots

Lechner has now translated her distinctive style into an unusual vase, composed of aluminium clips held together by stainless steel bolts. Stems can be slotted into the clips, which are supported by a base that can be filled with water.

“Exo 01 approaches the vase more as a support structure than as a container,” explained Lechner. “Inspired by braces used to hold and align parts of the body, the work applies this principle to flowers.”

Anne Holtrop is known for his rough-hewn furniture pieces, which conjure images of volcanic craters and mountainous landscapes.

For his inaugrual exhibition with Carpenter’s Workshop Gallery in London, the Dutch architect and designer is showing off his Low-relief collection of tables made from cast glass.

Their unrefined legs were informed by stone reliefs Holtrop visited in Aswan, Egypt.

Helsinki designer Didi Ng Wing Yin is known for his distinctively pleated wooden furniture, which he makes from locally sourced Finnish timber.

Last week, the designer debuted his first cabinet at Paris’s Spazio Nobile Gallery. Made from a mixture of fir and pine, finished with tung oil, the cabinet features a delicately pleated door made using Ng’s combined splitting, brushing and carving technique.

“I wanted to explore the dynamic contrast between form and texture,” Ng told Dezeen.

“The chunky pedestal base is built from straightforward architectural beams that retain their natural knots and raw characteristics, providing a heavy, structural anchor for the light, organic silhouette of the pleated cabinet door.”

One of many design events in October was PAD London, a collectible fair that takes place annually in Mayfair’s Berkley Square.

Among this year’s exhibitors was Mexico-based Manu Bañó, who showed a duo of striking patinated brass chairs formed from stacked, sculptural slabs of metal.

The chairs are a continuation of Bañó’s existing brass and stainless steel furniture, and were presented as part of the Objects with Narratives exhibition.

South Korean designer Seungjin Yang has been making playful furniture shaped like balloons for years, using colourful epoxy resin.

At PAD London, Yang showed his most recent balloon-like creations in the form of a sofa, two armchairs and two stools.

The designer coats real balloons in resin, painstakingly building their strength. Each piece is complete after around two weeks of delicate testing.

Don’t be misled by the intriguingly delicate appearance of Yang’s finished pieces, which are solid enough to be sat on.

#9205. Guillaume Cerutti named president of the Palace of Versailles

After eight months without a president, the Palace of Versailles finally has a new leader. Guillaume Cerutti, 60, has been named the president of the prestigious institution, according to the newspaper Politico. A graduate of France’s elite École nationale d’administration (ENA) and a former senior civil servant in the finance ministry, he succeeds Christophe Leribault, who was appointed president and director of the Louvre in February following the abrupt departure of Laurence des Cars.

The appointment marks Cerutti’s return to public service after two decades in the private sector. In a twist of fate, he is following in the footsteps of his former mentor, Jean-Jacques Aillagon, who headed the Palace and National Estate of Versailles from 2007 to 2011. Cerutti worked closely with Aillagon for many years, first at the Centre Pompidou, where Aillagon was the president from 1996 to 2002, and later as his chief of staff when Aillagon became France’s culture minister in 2002. “Having worked alongside Guillaume [Cerutti] for decades, I know he has all the experience and qualities needed to lead Versailles,” Aillagon told Le Monde.

Cerutti went on to put his management skills to work in the art market, becoming head of Sotheby’s France in 2007. In 2015, he was poached by François Pinault, who appointed him president of Christie’s operations in Europe, the Middle East, Russia and India. Just months later, he was promoted to global chief executive of the auction house. At both Sotheby’s and Christie’s, Cerutti built a reputation as a formidable cost-cutter. He also proved adept at steering Christie’s through difficult market conditions.

His next move within the Pinault empire, however, was less successful. In January 2025, Cerutti was appointed president of the Pinault Collection, which oversees the Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana in Venice, as well as the Bourse de Commerce in Paris. Once again, he was following in the footsteps of Aillagon, who had held the same position in the 2010s. But, as Le Monde reports, Cerutti’s efforts to impose the kind of financial discipline he had introduced at Christie’s, coupled with his wish to slow the pace of acquisitions, brought him into conflict with Pinault, who was used to running his collection on his own terms. Barely a year later, Cerutti was forced to step down.

He now assumes one of the most coveted positions in French cultural life, taking charge of a historic palace, museum and gardens that welcomed 8.4 million visitors in 2025 and employ around 1,000 people. His extensive connections in the worlds of business, culture and politics could prove particularly valuable as Versailles faces mounting budgetary pressures and an ever-greater need to secure support from wealthy patrons.

Two decades since the billionaire started planning a home for his collection in the French capital, the spectacular space is due to open on 23 January

The news follows his sudden departure as president of the Pinault Collection

The former chief executive officer of Christie’s moved to Paris to focus on the collection and its museums in 2025

He will be replaced by the president of Christie's America, Bonnie Brennan

#9204. Saype Is a Humanist Land Artist Who Captures His Murals with a Drone

Saype Is a Humanist Land Artist Who Captures His Murals with a Drone

Grass, snow, sand, and laterite—these are the surfaces Saype (real name Guillaume Legros) has spent the last fifteen years exploring, creating monumental, ephemeral works of art around the world with his 100% biodegradable paint.

The concept behind this 37-year-old Franco-Swiss former nurse—now one of the most prominent figures in contemporary international land art—is unique. “In the history of art, I haven’t found anyone who has produced what I do. I’ve looked,” he insists with a laugh. “Of course, the Lascaux caves come to mind, but it’s not the same scale or the same logic.”

His site-specific murals, ranging from 1,000 to 18,000 square meters, are exposed to the elements, local erosion, and regrowing vegetation, conveying messages of social commitment that he carefully preserves through aerial drone photography. From the very beginning, Saype has made his goal clear: “to influence mindsets without harming nature.”

His love for art began at age fourteen when he discovered street art and the paintings of Claude Monet and J.M.W. Turner. “It really resonated with me right away, and I started painting on canvas,” he explains. “When I was 18, I told my mom I wanted to be an artist. She replied, ‘No way, find a real job.’ In the end, it served me well to have responsibilities and lead a team as a nurse. I didn’t need to worry about making money or selling things to pursue art. That gave me greater creative freedom to do what I wanted.”

This nature enthusiast, who spent ten years studying environmental science and confronted mortality in his work as a nurse, soon asked himself the pivotal question: “What mark will I leave behind as a testament to my existence?” The turning point came in 2012, when he was 23. His approach is both intellectual and strategic. “I realized that if I want to make a living from my art and become an artist, I have to be well-known. And to achieve that, I have to invent something; otherwise, it becomes difficult to stand out from the crowd. That’s why I wanted to create my own biodegradable paint.”

Saype immersed himself in books on traditional recipes, watched dozens of documentaries, and tested around fifty different pigments. “I had to figure out how to orient myself in the space and spray my natural pigments onto the ground using industrial compressors. It had to be opaque enough on the grass, last long enough to withstand rain, wind, or snow, and not disappear right away even under normal conditions.”

His very first work, “L’Amour,” covering 1,600 square meters, came to life in 2015 in the French Alps. On the grass, he depicted a woman’s torso in a figurative style blending hyperrealism and Impressionism. Media coverage was immediate. The following year, Saype left his job in public health to devote himself fully to his artistic career, spending three years refining his technique. With a clear vision and an innovative concept, his work rapidly gained recognition, launching his international career.

Depending on the location and weather, there are “a thousand different recipes,” as he puts it. His ingredients typically include charcoal, chalk, casein (a milk protein that acts as a natural binder), and materials found on-site. Today, he works with a four-person team: two production assistants—childhood friends who have been with him since his first piece—a manager who aids in strategic decision-making, and a project manager handling back-office operations.

His murals, regardless of size, take two years to prepare, four to five days to execute, and one to two weeks to fade away. Among his most grueling creations, the project in Brazil tops the list: a 6,000-square-meter piece scaled down to 1,500 square meters, which he had to repaint three times due to severe weather. It is part of his famous “Beyond Walls” series—the world’s largest human chain, launched in 2019—which depicts intertwined hands to explore the forces that unite and divide humanity.

“I had just finished the piece in Benin, the departure point for slaves heading to Brazil or the Caribbean. I wanted to symbolically build this bridge in Copacabana. I had two parties to convince: UNESCO and the mayor of Rio de Janeiro. After a year of discussions, I was granted five days. It was complicated because of the COVID-19 pandemic. The forecast called for perfect weather, but it poured, and I had to start all over again after two days that had already been physically grueling. This triggered a domino effect, because I had three stages planned in Brazil and hadn’t accounted for enough pigments. I saw my project falling apart. In the end, I divided the surface area into four parts, which allowed me to complete the mural in a single day and have enough pigments left for the other two destinations.”

The visual impact of these ephemeral creations is elevated by drone footage, allowing them to reach a global audience. His creative process involves extensive research and hours on Google Earth to digitally map out each piece. During an initial drone flight, he surveys the terrain and plays with sightlines to position the artwork in situ. From this aerial perspective, he determines elevation, sets GPS coordinates, and places ground markers.

“I also create a small anamorphosis,” he explains. “This technique allows me to distort the perspective and establish a viewing angle. To set it up, I need to understand how the vanishing lines are positioned on the ground. I create a large square where I place stakes every fifteen meters, which gives me the proportions of the site.”

This framework allows him to prepare his sketch while adapting to the terrain. “I know the size of the artwork thanks to the planning beforehand, including the right amount of pigments. Everything has to be calculated roughly to avoid surprises. I have a 50% margin of error for pigments.” Lighting is another critical factor in his process. “If I shoot against the light, the mural won’t stand out the same way. So I play with different lighting conditions. If the child in the drawing is looking at the horizon, I’ll be more likely to choose a sunset.”

Saype uses a 4 kg DJI Inspire 2 drone with a 16 mm lens for his photography, carefully framing each shot while his assistant handles the flight controls. He started out in the 2010s using a DJI Phantom 1 with a GoPro taped underneath. “Drones were just becoming more widespread back then. There was no live video feed yet—everything was done on the fly,” he recalls with a laugh. “I’d take burst shots because we couldn’t see the results—it was complicated. Today, everything’s become much simpler. Google Earth was nothing like it either. I really worked differently back then.” As for AI, he limits its use to site research and administrative tasks.

Between equipment and paint, the initial investment runs roughly €50,000 each. “And that’s not even counting the ten compressors, valued at 10,000 euros each,” he adds jokingly. His projects fall into two categories: personal endeavors and professional collaborations with partners and patrons. He holds a six-year contract with Villars-sur-Ollon, a Swiss ski resort situated 1,300 meters high overlooking Lake Geneva. “Half the people who go there come to see my murals. I usually have free rein.”

His large-scale project “Beyond Walls” is entirely self-funded. The same goes for his mural in Giverny, France—a 10,000-square-meter water lily piece created on lawn to mark the centennial of Claude Monet’s death—as well as the artwork he designed for Handicap International in Gurten Park, Switzerland, celebrating 30 years of humanitarian action.

This year, Saype made his first foray into film. Partnering with Paramount, he created a 2,000-square-meter mural in the pastures of Beaufortain, Savoie, depicting a human hand reaching toward a dog’s paw. The piece appears in David Ayer’s *Heart of the Beast*, starring Brad Pitt. “I met the director of Paramount at one of my exhibitions. This film resonated with my artistic vision. I worked on a theme broader than the screenplay: man and animal, man and the living world. The choice of Savoie in France was quite similar to the atmosphere of Alaska, where the action takes place, because there is no human infrastructure. It feels like you’re at the end of the world.”

Following the completion of a site-specific work, signed and numbered prints on matte fine art paper (40×60 cm and 120×80 cm) are offered for sale on his website. He also creates unique physical pieces for galleries and museums. “Before painting the mural, I place 50×50 square centimeters of paper where I’m going to paint. And before taking the final photographs, I remove these pieces of paper. It’s the only physical trace left behind, created by nature, the elements, and the climate. I’ve been using this process since 2023. These fragments of the artwork form small squares that I’ve called ‘pixels.’ And collectors buy them. They’re one-of-a-kind.”

Saype is currently focusing on the United States amid growing social divides. He recently wrapped up a project in San Francisco—his second U.S. location after Minneapolis and his twenty-third worldwide, following stops in Paris, Berlin, Cape Town, Belfast, Fuji, Montreal, and Yamoussoukro (his largest mural to date, spanning 18,000 square meters).

“It’s no coincidence that I started with Minneapolis,” he says. “In 2022, George Floyd was murdered, and that sparked the Black Lives Matter movement. In January 2026, two killings of American citizens by ICE agents sparked a major social movement. In my view, San Francisco is at the center of the storm when it comes to AI issues. It has been said that there is a more than 10% chance that AI will destroy humanity in the coming decade—not to mention the resulting social upheaval.”

Between 2027 and 2030, he plans to roll out an American chapter of “Beyond Walls,” targeting roughly a dozen cities including Chicago, Austin, Detroit, Los Angeles, New York, St. Louis, and Miami. He aims for twelve stops over three years, beginning with two or three murals in 2027. His next destination is Montgomery, Alabama, to explore themes of civil rights. “The spot I’ve chosen that best showcases my artwork is in front of the State Capitol, whose park measures 100 meters by 50.”

When considering the future of humanity and land art, Saype feels both concerned and hopeful. Children are a recurring motif in his work, embodying the promise of a kinder world amidst rapid global change. “I feel a sense of mission in my work because I have an artistic voice that carries weight in terms of visual impact on society. I am deeply convinced that we will face unprecedented and unique choices. I always try to frame my messages in a positive light, even when addressing fundamental issues that remain complex. I think it harder to create beauty, nuance, and poetry than to make provocative art that forces people to question.”

Faced with global warming, landslides, tornadoes, and widespread flooding, the artist is mindful of his carbon footprint and actively seeking ways to limit air travel. Still, Saype remains optimistic about the future of land art: “Land artists will have plenty to say and share about this ever-changing landscape.”

#9201. Nature Photography Benefit with Thousands of Dollars in Giveaways Will Livestream on Saturday

Nature Photography Benefit with Thousands of Dollars in Giveaways Will Livestream on Saturday

The North American Nature Photography Association (NANPA) will host its annual half-day event, NANPA LIVE, on Saturday, November 7, 2026, offering a free global livestream from 3:00 to 6:00 PM PT that includes giveaways worth thousands of dollars.

The giveaways are free to enter. No purchase or donation necessary. Open to legal residents of the 50 United States and DC, 18 or older. Entries close Saturday, November 7, at 5:50 PM PT. Official Rules.

Nature photography enthusiasts worldwide can tune in without prior registration via YouTube, Facebook, or the organization’s website. For those unable to watch the initial broadcast live, the full recording will remain accessible on YouTube and the NANPA website afterward.

The program highlights major achievements across the field, featuring presentations from distinguished photographers Lynda Richardson, Dave Showalter, and Robert Glenn Ketchum. Throughout the afternoon, NANPA will present its 2026 Career and Service Awards, share stories from the Nature Photography Foundation, and offer an exclusive preview of the upcoming NANPA Summit 2027 in Savannah, Georgia. The event culminates in the live reveal of the 2027 NANPA Showcase winning images.

“NANPA LIVE puts a whole year of nature photography on one stage, from the people we’re honoring to the NANPA Showcase winners nobody has seen yet,” said Thomas Maddrey, who leads NANPA as CEO of ASMP. “Keeping it free to watch and free to enter means anyone who loves this work can be part of the afternoon.”

Maddrey emphasizes that keeping the broadcast entirely free allows anyone who loves nature photography to participate in celebrating the community’s work.

“Seeing this community come together is inspiring, and we want everyone to come and be part of this celebration. Win prizes, support the Nature Photography Foundation, and see some incredible images and presentations all in one place,” ASMP COO Melanie Porter adds.

Alongside the program, legal U.S. residents aged 18 and older can enter a free giveaway featuring thousands of dollars in prizes contributed by NANPA and its industry partners. Prize draws will occur in four sets live during the broadcast, though winners will also be notified via email within 24 hours. Entries remain open online until 5:50 PM PT on Saturday.

NANPA LIVE directly benefits the Nature Photography Foundation, an organization that funds conservation grants, educational initiatives, and college photography scholarships. To support these programs, an online silent auction runs through Sunday, November 15, at 6:00 PM PT. Auction lots feature signed fine art prints and books from renowned photographers Art Wolfe, Joel Sartore, and Thomas D. Mangelsen, as well as an exclusive spot in a sold-out New Mexico hummingbird photography workshop and a VIP package for two to the 2027 Savannah Summit. Direct donations are also welcomed through the foundation’s giving page.

#9199. Tiered immigration hub by Aedas opens at Shenzhen-Hong Kong border

Photography courtesy of Aedas (unless stated otherwise)

Architecture studio Aedas has completed a tiered, round-edged building designed to accommodate an immigration hub between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, China.

Perched on the banks of the Shenzhen River, the New Huanggang Port Development opened earlier this month in replacement of the original Huanggang Port, which first opened between the two cities in 1989.

Conceived by Aedas as a “large-scale integrated hub”, the nine-storey facility combines border control and transport networks with 25,000 square metres of public space.

Its stacked volume is complete with a “flowing facade” formed of horizontal metal fins, while its rounded form was designed to evoke a pebble, in reference to its riverside location.

“The grounded, rounded form responds to the building’s large scale and waterfront setting, evoking a pebble resting on the banks of the Shenzhen River,” the studio told Dezeen.

“Flowing metal fins wrap the elevation like ribbons, reinforcing the building’s fluid appearance and symbolising the close connection between Shenzhen and Hong Kong.”

“[The building’s] integrated transport networks, flowing facade and welcoming civic spaces express the close relationship between the two cities while establishing a distinctive point of arrival,” the studio added.

A modular, prefabrication approach was employed to construct the building’s volume, which opens up at ground level via two sunken plazas and is topped with a solar panel-covered roof terrace.

Across its four elevations, its rhythmic horizontal fins have been lifted to form large glass curtain walls that draw daylight into the interior.

Inside, the hub’s transport, immigration and public programmes are stacked vertically and connected by a network of internal escalators.

To accommodate an expected average of 200,000 passengers per day, two of these floors have been dedicated to immigration halls complete with a “barrier-free” design.

Direct connections to transport networks are provided on the floors below, where the hub links to four of Shenzhen’s rail and metro lines to “support a seamless border-crossing journey”.

“Transport, immigration and public programmes are vertically organised under one roof,” the studio said.

“The nine-storey building uses vertical stacking to organise pedestrian crossing, vehicle crossing, public transport and civic amenities efficiently within a constrained site, separating passenger and vehicular flows while maintaining convenient connections between programmes,” it added.

A series of structural, arched columns informed by Shenzhen’s emblem flower – the Bougainvillea – divide the expansive interiors, which are illuminated by 73 roof skylights, facade openings and an integrated lighting system.

Nearby, RHSP has unveiled designs for a skyscraper with a “striking butterfly layout” and MAD has completed a series of boulder-like galleries across a green-roofed museum.

#9198. Small Prints, Big Charm: Giving Fujifilm Instax Mini Its Due

Small Prints, Big Charm: Giving Fujifilm Instax Mini Its Due

It’s about time that the diminutive king of instant film got some Film Friday love, so we are giving this week’s spotlight over to Fujifilm’s Instax Mini color instant film and sharing why we love these small prints (and why you should as well).

To give you a sense of how popular Instax Mini is among our own staff, a month ago when we were asking staff for samples of the Instax Wide film, we had one staff member step forward with images for Film Friday. This week, while collecting Instax Mini samples, we had three of our staff bring in substantial collections of Instax Mini photos… and we had only directly asked one of those three to do so; the other two volunteered themselves. Maybe this isn’t as telling for you as it is for us. Sometimes it can be a bit difficult to corral our staff into providing sample images for these Film Fridays, so the enthusiasm with which they presented their Instax Mini shots was very revealing. And as many of you know, anything that our passionate staff is excited about when it comes to film photography is something worth taking note of.

Fuji Instax Mini is a pretty noteworthy film. The Mini format was the first of the Instax films, and it arrived on the scene in 1998. That’s right, Instax Mini has been around for over 20 years. But that isn’t where Instax film actually started. Fuji was in the business of manufacturing instant film as far back as the 1980s. Naturally, as Polaroid film gained popularity, other companies looked to emulate that magical instant film. Both Kodak and Fuji pursued their own versions of instant films, which quickly led to Kodak being sued by Polaroid and losing a lawsuit for infringing on Polaroid’s patents. Fuji, on the other hand, reached an agreement with Polaroid to be able to produce its own instant films as long as it didn’t market them in North America. Additionally, Fuji entered into a technology-sharing agreement with Polaroid whereby Fuji helped Polaroid develop magnetic recording media while Polaroid shared instant film technology with Fuji. All this is to say that by the time Fuji Instax arrived in 1998, Fuji had years of both experience and engineering put into the film, which explains why it is so good.

As referenced above, Fuji Instax was initially only well known in Asian markets. It wasn’t until Polaroid announced the discontinuation of its film in 2008 that Fuji decided to start marketing Instax films in North America. This gave them a valuable head start over the Impossible Project, which came along in 2010. Fuji Instax is still more popular in Asian markets than it is in North America and Europe, but that has been steadily evening out. These days, it is not uncommon at all to walk into a hip coffee shop and notice a wall of Instax photos pinned up, or see the film on sale at trendy stores next to chic clothing. Instax Mini has enjoyed a long and fruitful run, and it doesn’t seem to be anywhere close to ending.

At its technical heart, Fuji Instax Mini is an ISO 800 color film that is roughly the size and shape of your average credit card. Fuji Instax follows a couple of major innovations that were actually introduced by that doomed Kodak instant film, namely that the film is exposed through the back of the sheet, allowing the cameras to forego the necessary mirror that would reverse the image. This allows Instax cameras to be much more compact. Also, Fuji builds the batteries and pressure plates into its cameras as opposed to the film cartridges, further helping to reduce the cost of each Instax sheet of film. What you end up with is a combination that is fun, relatively inexpensive, and works quite well.

All that history and technical info is really only there to set the stage for you and give you a bit more appreciation for the Instax name. What is really going to jump out at you when you start using Instax Mini film is how good it looks. It is crisp, sharp, and saturated. You get lovely images from Instax, and the film performs quite consistently. There really isn’t much more to say in that regard. It just looks very, very good, virtually every single time. This may help explain why so many of our staff like carrying these cameras around. Unlike the Instax Wide, which essentially uses the same film, the Instax Mini is much more portable, and the resulting shots can fit in your wallet. When we started sifting through the samples our staff brought in, we quickly noticed that they use Instax Mini to record their lives. We have images from nights out, Halloween parties, poignant (or hilarious) moments from home life, and the like. We got in a couple of landscapes, but really the majority of the images were about personal lives. The Instax Mini is a really great camera for this purpose. Yes, you can make artful landscapes, still lifes, or portraits with it, but that is not the raison d’être for this film… or what inspires most Instax photographers to use it.

For proof of this, check out the images in our samples of the young boy shaving and with his first washed dish (a spoon). Both of these images were brought in by our lab manager, David, showing a couple of memorable moments he experienced helping to raise his stepson, Cash. He chose to grab his Instax Mini over all his other cameras, then added the handwritten notes after the prints ejected to provide a bit of historical context to go with the images. Sure, he could have shot negative film, waited to finish the roll, had it developed and printed, and made the same notes on the back of the 4x6s he eventually received, but that would have taken days, if not weeks. He had these keepsakes within moments. And that is the largest part of the charm that this film has to offer. You can carry these cameras everywhere. They are easy to use. The prints eject right out the top of the camera and develop within a few minutes. The image forms as if by magic right in front of your eyes. You have instant keepsakes to go along with all those fun moments.

Fuji Instax film is available in both color and monochrome versions. Both emulsions are a fast ISO 800, and both feature visibly smooth grain. Both have beautiful contrast, with the color film offering punchy colors and the monochrome offering rich tonality from shadows to highlights. And just to make things even more fun, Fuji produces this film with a plethora of odd or colorful borders, such as the contact sheet version of the Instax Mini.

And that is our pitch/take/review of the Fuji Instax Mini. It doesn’t get taken terribly seriously. Perhaps it should be, but maybe it shouldn’t. It is fun to shoot with, but also has the capability to make images that might end up meaning more to you than any you make with your other cameras. Even after decades of using various instant films, the magic of watching instant film develop never quite wears off. At the very least, it is a process quite different from what you get working with your 35mm or medium-format cameras.

We will have Fuji Instax Mini film on sale today, both color and monochrome. Pay a visit to our website or our Portland, Oregon shop and take advantage of our one-day sale. All you will need then will be an Instax Mini camera, but don’t fret, as we have those too!

#9196. Meike Mixes It Up On APS-C With New $449 58mm f/1.2 Portrait Prime

Meike Mixes It Up On APS-C With New $449 58mm f/1.2 Portrait Prime

Meike has announced yet another addition to its Mix series of primes, and this time it’s a portrait prime for APS-C mirrorless cameras. The Meike 58mm f/1.2 Mix is a fast $449 prime for Sony, Fujifilm, and Nikon mirrorless systems.

The Meike 58mm f/1.2 Mix includes 14 elements arranged across 10 groups and an 11-bladed aperture diaphragm. Meike promises “soft, smooth bokeh” and “fine detail.” While it’s impossible to say for sure whether the image quality is good with this new lens, the Mix series has proven effective so far in PetaPixel‘s hands-on testing.

With the approximately 1.5x crop factor on APS-C mirrorless cameras, the 58mm prime delivers an angle of view more like an 87mm (or roughly 85mm) prime lens on full-frame cameras. This is a very popular focal length for portraits, and one Meike already caters to on full-frame cameras with its 85mm f/1.4 Mix II AF STM.

Meike doesn’t specify what type of autofocus system its new portrait prime uses, but it promises fast autofocus that works alongside in-camera detection modes like eye-detect and face-detect AF. The lens focuses as close as 0.62 meters (just over two feet).

The Meike Mix series typically uses a straightforward, unassuming design, and this one is no different. However, while the black lens looks pretty standard, the lens also comes in more striking silver, white, and white-and-black colorways.

The lens is 90 millimeters (3.5 inches) long and has a 62mm filter thread. The lens weighs about 450 grams (15.9 ounces) on E and X mount, but the Nikon Z lens is a bit heavier at 455 grams (just over a pound). This is likely because the Nikon Z mount has a wider diameter. In any event, they’re all compact and lightweight.

The Meike AF 58mm f/1.2 Mix actually faces quite a bit of competition.

Sigma makes a 56mm f/1.4 DC DN Contemporary lens for APS-C Sony, Fujifilm, and Nikon cameras, plus other ones like Canon RF and L-Mount. It’s $454 right now thanks to a $125 holiday savings discount. While not quite as fast as Meike’s new lens, it offers a similar focal length and is much lighter at just 280 grams (9.9 ounces). It’s also a lot shorter, measuring just 59.5 millimeters (2.3 inches) long.

The Viltrox AF 56mm f/1.2 Pro is as fast as Meike’s new lens, but it’s over 100 grams heavier and ever-so-slightly longer. It’s available for $522 thanks to a 10% holiday discount on Sony E, Fujifilm X, and Nikon Z. This is probably the closest competitor to Meike.

For much less money, Viltrox also offers the AF 56mm f/1.7 lens. It’s slower, of course, but compact, lightweight, and just $180. It’s also on the same three mounts: E, X, and Z.

For Meike’s part, its new lens is $449, putting it just below the discounted Sigma 56mm f/1.4 and a fair bit less than Viltrox’s speedy f/1.2 prime. The Meike 58mm f/1.2 Mix is available now through Meike. While it’s not yet listed at B&H at the time of writing, it should be available there soon.

#9195. Art Collaboration Kyoto fair celebrates six years of matchmaking galleries

The sixth edition of Art Collaboration Kyoto includes 52 galleries in the main section and 11 galleries in the Kyoto Meetings section Courtesy Art Collaboration Kyoto

This year marks the sixth edition of Art Collaboration Kyoto (ACK), the fair that pairs Japanese commercial galleries with international peers to collaborate on shared stands. The fair will take place from 7 to 9 November at the Kyoto International Conference Center. The event has become known for its distinctive exhibitor model, which has proved popular with exhibitors and fair attendees alike.

“We thought, ‘If we are going to do this, why not create a fair that galleries and artists themselves would find exciting and genuinely want to be part of?’” Miho Doi, ACK’s director of experiences, tells The Art Newspaper about the fair’s founding.

This year’s edition includes a number of high-profile Western galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Jeffrey Deitch and Carlos Ishikawa, alongside Asian galleries such as Seoul’s Gallery Hyundai.

The collaborative format is intended to give both Japanese and international galleries an opportunity to work together and introduce their artists and programmes to new audiences. Pairing domestic and foreign galleries has been key for the success of the fair, organisers say, especially for dealers without experience in Japan.

“For an overseas gallery, participating independently in an art fair in a country it is entering for the first time is by no means easy,” Doi says. “We have heard from participating galleries that, for a variety of reasons, taking part in a Japanese fair entirely on their own would not have been realistic.”

The fair’s main section will bring together 52 galleries. Taro Nasu from Tokyo will join forces with Hauser & Wirth for a presentation focused on text in contemporary art, including works by Louise Bourgeois, Jenny Holzer, David Horvitz and Glenn Ligon, among others. Nanzuka from Tokyo will work alongside Jeffrey Deitch, while Tokyo Gallery + BTAP will team up with Gallery Hyundai for a presentation pairing post-war Japanese and Korean experimental practices, including the Korean artist Seung-taek Lee in dialogue with the Japanese artist Kishio Suga.

“Some participating galleries have even described ACK as a ‘fair built on friendship’ rather than a place for competition,” Doi says.

Another section of the fair is dedicated to presentations from 11 individual galleries with strong connections to Kyoto. Mendes Wood DM, for instance, will present works by Tomie Ohtake—who was born in Kyoto and later relocated to São Paulo, which is home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan—among other artists. Hong Kong’s Kiang Malingue will show works by Yang Chi-Chuan and Faye Wei Wei, whose sculptures and paintings respond to Kyoto’s landscapes and urban environment.

A joint stand with Nonaka-Hill and Hoffman Donahue galleries Courtesy Art Collaboration Kyoto

The fair also coincides with a programme of special exhibitions and projects across Kyoto. This year, the Scottish painter Andrew Cranston will present an installation at Ryosokuin Temple, a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto’s historic Gion district. The exhibition is organised by Modern Art and Ingleby. Elsewhere, Carlos Ishikawa will stage a presentation of work by Evelyn Taocheng Wang and Issy Wood at Korin-in Temple.

This edition of ACK takes place under a new leadership committee structure, introduced earlier this year. Rather than being led by a single fair director, ACK is now guided by a seven-member committee with expertise spanning art consulting, cultural foundations, Kyoto cultural policy, fair production, education, partnerships and collector relations. The former fair director, Yukako Yamashita, now leads the fair’s ambassador programme.

As for ACK’s next six years, Doi says the leadership committee aims to develop the fair into a platform that “connects the art scenes of Japan and the world and generates a virtuous cycle between cultural and commercial value”.

The fifth edition of the fair, where Japanese galleries invited international ones to share stands, welcomed 72 exhibitors

The fair's third edition has expanded in size since last year

Art Collaboration Kyoto brings together Japanese and international galleries during a city-wide celebration of the arts

The fair’s Presents section for younger galleries, often among its most vibrant sectors, features bold stands organised by ambitious dealers who understand the costs of doing business

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($24,500 in 2026), HSA ($4,400 individual / $8,750 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2026, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $24,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

If you are 40 with $50,000 saved and feeling behind, shifting from a 10% savings rate to a 40% savings rate on a $100,000 income adds $30,000 per year to your investment accounts. At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

Add up every 401(k), IRA, Roth IRA, HSA, and other retirement account balance. Include employer-sponsored plans from previous jobs — many people have orphaned 401(k) accounts they have forgotten about. Exclude your home equity and Social Security for now.

Use the age-bracket tables above to see where you stand. If you are above the median, you are ahead of most Americans your age. If you are below, calculate exactly how far behind and what it would take to catch up.

Most employers allow you to change your 401(k) contribution rate at any time. Increasing by 2% of salary is small enough that you will barely notice the paycheck reduction, but it compounds dramatically over time. Repeat this increase every six months until you are maxing out your 401(k).

Roughly one in four employees leaves free employer match money on the table. If your employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary, you need to contribute at least 6% to capture the full match. This is an instant 50% return on your money — no investment can beat it.

A Roth IRA provides tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, with no required minimum distributions. The 2026 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+). If your income exceeds the Roth limits, use the backdoor Roth conversion strategy to contribute indirectly.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The national median for under-35 is only $13,000, so if you have more than that, you are already ahead of most peers.

The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

Generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

It is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $72,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

#9192. Please Do Not Buy Costco’s $520 Canon R100 Kit

Please Do Not Buy Costco’s $520 Canon R100 Kit

The holiday season is ramping up and that once again means Canon is trotting out the same cash cow it has milked for the last three straight years. Costco (soon to be followed by other stores, surely) is offering a Canon EOS R100 kit for an enticing $520. Do not buy it.

Consider this a public service announcement, and a reiteration of the same plea I published two years ago (except, somehow, the R100 is more expensive now!). The only reason to buy the Canon EOS R100 is that it is cheap. Like, cheap cheap. It is easily the most affordable interchangeable lens mirrorless camera that you can buy brand-new right now, but that is quite literally the only thing it has going for it.

As an investment in someone’s future in photography, it is a terrible purchase.

“Using the R100 felt like going a few steps backward in camera technology. Yes, it’s simple in its intention and design, but maybe a little too simple,” Chris Niccolls wrote in his review. “Even significantly older cameras than the R100 outperform it. I don’t think I would recommend this camera to many people unless the budget had to remain absolutely fixed at sub-$500. Even then, I would probably just stick to my smartphone.”

We've been particularly harsh on what we call "toy cameras" lately, and those are basically any compact camera that repurposes what are glorified dashcam sensors and crams them into plastic camera-shaped bodies. Those are e-waste waiting to happen. The R100 is not e-waste in the sense that it is a camera that does take decent photos and features a removable battery. It is better than a piece of garbage, but the benchmark for a $500+ purchase should be significantly higher than "not garbage." There are better options out there that are within the same price tier.

While the R100 wins as the cheapest, there are three cameras that are better that can be purchased brand-new today for around the same price.

82 PixelMeter Nikon Z30 Reviewer Consensus: Strong The Nikon Z30 is a compact, user-friendly mirrorless camera designed primarily for vloggers and content creators who prioritize video production. While it excels at capturing sharp 4K video with reliable autofocus and a convenient vari-angle screen, it lacks an electronic viewfinder and in-body stabilization, making it less suitable for dedicated stills photography. Nikon Z30Buy new on B&HNikon Z30Buy used on KEH.com

First, let's consider the Nikon Z30. While it isn't perfect, it is a substantially better camera. While it does not have an electronic viewfinder, unlike the R100, it does feature a fully articulating rear touchscreen, is smaller and lighter than the R100, takes great video, and has excellent autofocus performance. It has a faster burst photo mode than the R100, has a good degree of ruggedness to it, and is overall a better feeling and operating camera. The Z30 is also substantially discounted versus its launch price: it costs under $600 now.

82 PixelMeter Canon EOS R50 Reviewer Consensus: Strong The Canon EOS R50 is a compact, entry-level mirrorless camera that offers impressive subject-tracking autofocus and sharp 4K video capabilities for beginners. While it serves as an excellent, user-friendly tool for content creators, its small form factor results in limited physical controls and a lack of in-body image stabilization. Canon EOS R50Buy new on B&HCanon EOS R50Buy used on KEH.com

Admittedly, the Z30 isn't the best photo-specific camera, so if that is more important to you when trying to find something better than the R100, then Canon's own R50 is just overall a better camera in every way. Everything that's wrong with the R100 is better on the R50: you get back an EVF, you get a fully articulating rear LCD, improved video features, and -- really importantly -- the R50 supports USB-C charging directly through the camera. One of the biggest drawbacks of the R100 is its lack of support for this, which makes traveling with the camera a hassle since you always have to carry the wall charger with you. The Canon R50 is available today for $679.

84 PixelMeter Canon EOS R50 V Reviewer Consensus: Strong The Canon EOS R50 V is a compact, video-centric mirrorless camera that provides creators with high-quality 4K output, 10-bit color, and convenient vertical shooting tools. Although it lacks in-body image stabilization and an electronic viewfinder, its reliable autofocus and accessible controls make it a strong entry point for those upgrading from smartphones. The R50V, which is a video-focused version of the R50, is also a great choice if you want to stick with Canon but won't miss a viewfinder and want to get even closer to the R100's price point. The R50V is basically the R50 with its EVF chopped off, and for that, it's available for $569.

I will admit, it is impossible to buy any other mirrorless camera brand-new that comes with a lens and memory card for $520. The lens Canon bundles with the R100 isn't good, but to get it separately costs $350. That means the R100 actually is worth just $170 as part of this kit. Again, this camera's only selling point is that it is cheap as dirt. But I beg you to find something that's affordable and also good.

Right now at KEH, you can get a Canon 5D Mark II in excellent condition for $296. You can then pick up a 24-105mm f/4L for $475 or the more entry-level option of 24-105mm f/3.5-5.6 for $256. Both options are slightly more expensive than Costco's kit, but are substantially better combos that will actually provide a burgeoning photographer with the ability to learn and grow. There are so many other possibilities on the used market, too. This is just one example.

Canon 5D Mark IIBuy used on KEH.comCanon EF 24-105mm f/4 L IS USMBuy used on KEH.comCanon EF 24-105mm f/3.5-5.6 IS STMBuy used on KEH.com

This all takes me back to my real main issue with the R100. It's barely fine as far as technology goes, but it is so limited that it serves as a poor camera to invest anything more than a first glance into the world of photography with. It cannot grow with someone beyond the very first stage of photography and after that, they're going to want one of these other cameras I've mentioned that costs just a little bit more. Why spend that amount twice? Skip the R100 stage and go for a camera that can support several years of interest, not just a few weeks.

I love photography. It would break my heart if the reason someone didn't realize they loved it too was because the experience of the R100 was so bland and uninteresting that they gave up on the hobby before it had time to take root.

#9191. Lacaton & Vassal wins Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027

The Créateurs Design Association & Awards has named Pritzker Prize-winning French studio Lacaton & Vassal Architectes the recipient of the Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes, which is led by architects Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal and known for its social housing designs, was recognised for contributing to contemporary architecture by transforming and improving existing buildings.

The Créateurs Design Associates (CDA) said the studio’s work improves “living conditions while preserving resources and architectural heritage”.

The duo said it was “very happy” to receive the award.

“Charlotte Perriand’s tireless pursuit of comfort, well-being, and the pleasure of the inhabitant and of everyday life, her modernity, and her political commitment to exposing poor housing conditions and to transmission and education remain profoundly relevant today and are a source of inspiration,” Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal said.

“Her manifest spirit of openness and freedom touches us deeply. We are very happy to receive this distinction.”

The architects founded their studio in 1989 and have since worked on high-profile projects such as the transformation of the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, the Nantes School of Architecture and the Cité du Grand Parc housing transformation in Bordeaux.

The latter, which was completed with Frédéric Druot and Christophe Hutin, won the European Union’s Mies van der Rohe Award in 2019.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes’ other social housing projects include the renovation of the 1960s Tour Bois-le-Prêtre tower block in Paris, also in collaboration with Frédéric Druot, which was completed in 2011.

It also converted and extended a former shipbuilding workshop to create the FRAC Nord-Pas de Calais contemporary art gallery in Dunkirk.

The Le Prix Charlotte Perriand was established in collaboration with the family of the late architect and recognises practitioners whose contributions have advanced architecture and design.

“In awarding Le Prix Charlotte Perriand to Lacaton & Vassal, the CDA members recognise the care and imagination with which they approach the places people call home. Their work shows how much can be gained by understanding what is already there,” Créateurs Design Association co-founder Meredith Xavier said.

The award will be given to Lacaton & Vassal Architectes in a ceremony on 16 January 2027, at the Shangri-La Paris. Architect Kengo Kuma will also be honoured at the event as the winner of the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award 2027.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes has previously won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2021, as well as the 2023 Soane Medal for architecture.

Last year, Lacaton won the 2025 Jane Drew Prize for women in architecture.

#9189. Motorola’s $1,599 Signature 27 Is the ‘World’s Fastest Android Smartphone’

Motorola’s $1,599 Signature 27 Is the ‘World’s Fastest Android Smartphone’

After numerous teases and even a sponsored YouTube hands-on video, Motorola has finally, thankfully, fully unveiled its new flagship smartphone, the Signature 27. It is being billed as the world’s fastest Android smartphone. It’s certainly among the most expensive slab phones.

The Motorola Signature 27 runs on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, Qualcomm’s leading mobile chip. It has an eight-core CPU, six performance cores, and a suite of advanced features. It’s seriously powerful.

And while that’s great, and performance is definitely a significant focus for the Motorola Signature 27, that’s only part of the story. Motorola is pulling out all the stops.

“The world’s best camera system launched in 2026, outranking all other Android and iOS devices, as assessed by DxOMark.”

“The brightest display available in a smartphone.”

“The only smartphone in-market with Audio by Bang & Olufsen.”

Looking first at the camera system claim, DxOMark did, in fact, rate the Motorola Signature 27 as the second-best smartphone camera system on the market, behind only the Huawei Pura 80 Ultra, which launched last year. The Signature 27 is just ahead of the Apple iPhone 18 Pro.

As PetaPixel has written a couple of times now, the Motorola Signature 27 has a 50-megapixel Sony Lytia 910 main camera with LOFIC technology, promising expanded dynamic range and better low-light image quality, all else equal. The Lytia 910 is a relatively large Type 1/1.28 image sensor that has proven very good in the few phones that feature it.

The Signature 27 also has a 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera with 100x Super Zoom and a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera. Motorola doesn’t say who makes these image sensors, but it does say the telephoto is a Type 1/1.56 and the ultrawide has a Type 1/2.76 sensor. These are fairly standard sizes among high-end phones.

But wait, it sure looks like there’s a fourth camera on the back of the Signature 27. Good eye, hypothetical person. This is the first ever dedicated “EVS action sensor” on a smartphone. EVS stands for “Event Vision Sensor,” and it detects pixel-level changes in light intensity in real time and works alongside Action Mode to freeze fast-action subjects more effectively. It’s like an assistant rather than a dedicated camera. It will be very interesting to see how well it works in the real world. PetaPixel plans to get its hands on the Signature 27 for a comprehensive review.

Then there’s the display, the world’s brightest. It’s a new 6.9-inch LTPO Extreme AMOLED that features Tandem OLED technology. It combines two emissive layers into one and promises up to 12,000 nits of peak brightness. Unsurprisingly, there’s a caveat. There always is. This is localized peak brightness, not full-screen brightness, and will almost assuredly be limited to very specific situations. Nonetheless, that’s crazy bright.

As for the claim that the Motorola Signature 27 is the only in-market phone with Audio by Bang & Olufsen, that’s pretty straightforward. Motorola recently signed a multi-year partnership with the audio brand, and the Signature 27 features B&O’s audio expertise in both hardware and software. Motorola touts an all-new speaker architecture that sounds truly fantastic.

To no one’s surprise, the premium, flagship Motorola Signature 27 will cost a pretty penny when it arrives on November 19. The Signature 27 is $1,599, which puts it near the very top of the slab phone price bracket, and certainly places it among the most expensive smartphones available in the U.S. Speaking of which, it’s great to see a high-end Android smartphone that isn’t made by Samsung or Google get an American release. They are few and far between.

#9186. Pioneering Female Photographer’s Work Discovered After Thousands of Negatives Found in Suitcase

Pioneering Female Photographer’s Work Discovered After Thousands of Negatives Found in Suitcase

The work of a pioneering female photographer, whose images remained hidden for decades until thousands of her negatives were discovered in suitcases, is being exhibited for the first time.

Violette Cornelius Rediscovered an upcoming exhibition at the Nederlands Fotomuseum in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, will bring together more than 200 works by Violette Cornelius (1919–1998), who was among the first generation of women to become professional photographers.

Based in Amsterdam, Cornelius was an active member of the artists’ resistance during World War II. She helped produce forged identity documents and documented the resistance movement through her photography. After the war, Cornelius worked in architectural photography, reportage, and photobooks. From the 1960s onward, she traveled to countries including Mali, Iraq, India, Yemen, and Peru, where she photographed the social impact of rapid urbanization.

By living and working among the people she photographed for extended periods, Cornelius developed an intimate and personal style. However, much of her work, particularly her international reportages, remained largely unknown for decades.

But in 2003, five years after Cornelius’ death, the Nederlands Fotomuseum received suitcases from her son containing thousands of negatives, slides, contact prints, and documents. A further discovery followed in June 2026, when five additional cases containing vintage prints, dummies, notes, and books were found.

Photo historians were astonished by the scale and quality of the photographs uncovered in Cornelius’ archive.

“We were astounded at the scale and quality of the work we encountered, work for which no place had yet been reserved in the canon of Dutch photography,” curator Loes van Harrevelt of the Nederlands Fotomuseum says of the discovery of Cornelius’ photo archive.

Cornelius’ photographs documenting resistance activities during World War II are now considered a unique visual record of the period. They have also been recognized as important heritage and included in UNESCO Nederland’s Memory of the World register.

Violette Cornelius Rediscovered will run at the Nederlands Fotomuseum from November 20, 2026, to February 28, 2027. The exhibition is the result of an extensive study of Cornelius’ life and work conducted by the museum and will feature more than 200 works. The exhibition will also coincide with the publication of the first monograph dedicated to Cornelius, bringing greater attention to a photographer whose work remained largely overlooked for decades.

#9185. Comment | John Berger at 100: why the writer and artist's legacy is as vital as ever

Tom Overton's biography John Berger: From Life was published in August this year

John Berger was born on 5 November 1926, making this year his centenary. Next year will be the tenth anniversary of his death. It seems a good time to look back and take stock of one of the 20th century’s most persuasive and challenging voices in art and literature, and one of only two writers on art who also wrote a Booker Prize-winning novel (the other was Anita Brookner).

The story of Berger’s 1972 Booker Prize speech, after winning for his novel G., is told by Tom Overton in his thoroughly engaging biography, John Berger: From Life, published in August this year. To a stunned and affronted audience at the prize ceremony, Berger announced he was donating half the considerable prize money to a British chapter of the Black Panthers, as a protest against the labour exploitation in British Guiana that had made the Booker McConnell fortune. It is hard to imagine an acceptance speech nowadays without acknowledgment of the reputation-laundering that is still widespread in cultural sponsorship. Berger’s bravery in making such a stand, which can hardly have been easy, is one aspect of his legacy worth remembering.

This legacy—why Berger matters—is the subject of the smattering of centenary events but is also brought into focus by their dearth. The only anniversary exhibition in Britain devoted to Berger is a small display of his drawings at Mandell’s Gallery in Norwich (until 21 November), co-curated by the artists John Christie and Martin Battye. Berger’s drawings are those of a writer intent on seeing the world around him, gathering images and experiences, but also of an artist who knows that the best way to look is to draw.

Berger’s popular legacy lies with his 1972 book Ways of Seeing, which remains, quite remarkably, a bestseller—“one of the most stimulating and influential books on art in any language”, says its publisher, Penguin. Anyone rereading the book now might pause at such a description. Berger was hardly the first to show how images are constructed by viewers, and reflect their prejudices, but he was the first to publish a book that communicated this idea so effectively, combining relentless polemic with brilliant design (thanks to Richard Hollis). It also helped that the book was based on a successful television series and contained numerous pin-up images to back up the argument that Old Master painting, through patterns of privilege and possession, relates directly to contemporary advertising.

Yet the arguments feel dated and even slack, quite unlike Berger’s later writing on art. His attacks on Seymour Slive’s interpretation of Frans Hals, and on Kenneth Clark’s book The Nude, are grounded in a personal dislike of art historians. What Gen Z art students will make of his attack on the “disingenuousness that bedevils the subject of art history”, picking apart Lawrence Gowing’s nitty argument that the figures in Gainsborough’s Mr and Mrs Andrews (around 1750) are not just enjoying nature but being philosophical about it, is anybody’s guess.

And yet the questions Berger asks about how we value works of art, and how they exist as part of our lives and the world in which we live, are still utterly relevant. They are part of what Overton describes as the idea central to all his writing: how we live with the dead, how the past surrounds us and keeps us company. Berger spent his life tilting against a world “ordered with the logic of profit, always looking forward, never back”, Overton writes, a world therefore bent on neglecting the past and forgetting the dead.

It is an idea explored in Berger’s short story The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol, from the novel Pig Earth, about peasant life in France at the turn of the 20th century. And it appears in the leaps of imagination and connections he draws between art from different periods in the writings collected in Portraits: John Berger on Artists: on Fayum portraits seen from a century of exile and emigration, or his description of drawing Antonello da Messina’s astonishing 1475 Christ Crucified in the National Gallery, while recalling hearing pianist Myra Hess playing in the same gallery in 1942 (before being thrown out for swearing at a security guard), or his account of Jean-François Millet, “a moralist in the only way a great artist can be, by the power of his identification with his subjects”, in his case the experience of peasants working the land.

Berger’s legacy is his remarkable ability to link art with the most important questions of our time, and so to redeem it from the clutches of the market and specialists alike.
