#9182. Wildlife Silhouettes and the Power of Shape

Wildlife Silhouettes and the Power of Shape

Explore how posture, shape, light, and composition can help wildlife photographers create striking backlit imagery that tells a powerful story.

Wildlife photography often emphasizes detail. Photographers work to capture the texture of feathers, patterns in an animal’s coat, expressions in its eyes, and the small features that reveal its character. Silhouette photography takes a different approach. Instead of relying on those details, it reduces an animal to its outline, using shape, posture, and positioning to communicate the subject. The result is a more graphic, interpretive image that asks viewers to recognize the animal through its form rather than its appearance.

Creating compelling wildlife silhouettes involves more than placing an animal in front of a bright sunset. The subject needs a recognizable outline, its posture should contribute to the image, and the background must provide enough contrast to make its shape clear. Composition and timing also matter more because small changes in an animal’s position can dramatically alter the photograph. Understanding these elements helps photographers recognize opportunities where removing detail can make a wildlife image more expressive.

A successful silhouette depends on how easily the viewer can identify the subject and interpret its position. Without visible detail, the outline becomes the primary source of information. Body proportions, head position, and distinctive anatomical features all contribute to whether an animal remains recognizable. A silhouette that communicates its subject immediately is generally more effective than one that leaves the viewer guessing.

Some animals and poses naturally lend themselves to this approach. An elk with clearly defined antlers, a fox with its ears raised, or a bird with its wings extended has a distinctive outline that remains identifiable even when rendered entirely dark. By contrast, an animal facing directly toward the camera may lose much of its recognizable shape. Its body can appear compressed, and important features may overlap.

A strong silhouette should also contribute something to the photograph beyond simply creating a dark subject. It might emphasize an animal’s scale against a large landscape, highlight a particular behavior, or simplify an otherwise busy scene. The most effective images use the silhouette as a deliberate storytelling choice rather than treating it as an exposure effect.

Before photographing an animal as a silhouette, consider which anatomical features make it recognizable. Different species have distinctive profiles, and understanding those features can help you anticipate the most effective shooting angle. For mammals, this might be the shape of the head, the length of the legs, the position of the ears, or features such as antlers and horns. For birds, the bill, neck, tail, and wing shape often provide the most important identifying characteristics.

The angle of the animal can change how these features appear. A broadside position often provides a recognizable profile because the body, head, and legs appear as separate shapes. A three-quarter angle can add depth, particularly when the animal turns its head toward the camera. Front-facing positions can also work, but they often rely on distinctive features to keep the outline from looking indistinct.

Birds offer a wide range of possibilities because their silhouettes change so dramatically with wing position. A bird in flight with its wings fully extended has a very different outline from one gliding with its wings angled downward. The shape of the wings can also help identify a species, with long, narrow wings, broad rounded wings, and separated flight feathers each creating different visual patterns.

Studying animal profiles and observing wildlife in the field can help you recognize these opportunities. Instead of focusing only on whether an animal is facing the right direction, look for positions that reveal its defining characteristics. A slight turn of the head or a change in ear position can be enough to transform an ordinary outline into a recognizable portrait.

When fine detail disappears, posture becomes one of the most important ways to communicate an animal’s character. A standing animal with its head lowered may create a relatively unremarkable shape, while the same animal raising its head, stretching, or interacting with another individual can produce a much more expressive image. The silhouette should ideally show something about the animal, not just document its presence.

Behavior can provide some of the most interesting opportunities. An elk bugling with its head raised, a bear standing on its hind legs, or a bird extending its wings during a display all create recognizable gestures. Even smaller movements can work well. A fox listening with its ears pointed forward, or a heron poised with its neck extended, can create a distinctive profile without requiring dramatic action.

Anticipating these moments is often more effective than reacting after they happen. Wildlife photographers already spend considerable time learning animal behavior to predict where subjects will move and when interesting activity might occur. The same preparation applies to silhouettes. If you know a bird is likely to take flight from a particular perch, or that an animal regularly pauses on an exposed ridge, you can prepare for the moment rather than scrambling to adjust your position after it begins.

Continuous shooting can help when the opportunity involves movement, but a burst of frames does not guarantee the strongest composition. Watch for the positions that communicate the behavior most clearly. For a bird in flight, that might mean waiting for the wings to reach full extension. For a mammal, it could be a moment when its head and limbs create a particularly expressive gesture. The goal is to capture the most meaningful position, not simply the most frames.

The simplicity of a silhouette makes compositional decisions especially noticeable. With fewer details competing for attention, the animal’s placement, direction, and relationship with the surrounding space carry much of the photograph’s visual weight.

Consider the direction in which the animal is looking or moving. Leaving open space in front of a subject can create a sense of movement and give the viewer somewhere to follow its gaze. A bird flying toward the open side of the frame, for example, generally feels less confined than one positioned directly against the edge. Similarly, an animal looking toward an open horizon can create a sense of anticipation or connection with the landscape.

The animal’s size within the frame also changes the story. A relatively large silhouette emphasizes anatomy and posture, making it easier to appreciate the subject’s shape. A smaller animal surrounded by open sky or landscape can communicate scale, distance, and isolation. This wider approach can be particularly effective when the environment is an important part of the photograph.

Natural lines can provide useful compositional structure. A ridgeline, shoreline, or distant tree line can anchor an animal within the scene and create a visual connection between the subject and its surroundings. Experiment with both tight and wide compositions when the situation allows. A tighter frame emphasizes the animal, while a wider image can reveal more about its place in the landscape.

Silhouette photography depends on contrast between the subject and its surroundings. Sunrise and sunset provide familiar opportunities because the sky is often much brighter than the landscape. Positioning an animal against a bright section of sky can create a dark outline while retaining the colors and tonal transitions of the surrounding light.

The sun does not necessarily need to be visible in the frame. A colorful band of light near the horizon, a bright opening between clouds, or a softly illuminated sky can all provide an effective background. Other lighting conditions can work as well. Bright overcast skies, open water, reflections, and distant illuminated areas of landscape may provide enough contrast to isolate an animal.

Think about the background as an active part of the composition rather than simply a source of brightness. A relatively uniform sky often works well because it allows the animal’s shape to stand out. More complex backgrounds can introduce atmosphere and context, but they may compete with the subject if they contain too many contrasting elements.

Light quality and direction change as the sun rises or sets, so the best background may be available only briefly. Identify promising positions before the animal reaches them, and watch how the light changes across the scene. A slight shift in the animal’s position or the sky’s color can produce a noticeably different result.

Even a distinctive animal can become difficult to identify when its outline merges with the surrounding environment. Branches, grasses, rocks, and other animals can obscure important features, particularly the legs, ears, antlers, and wings. Because a silhouette removes most internal detail, these overlaps matter more than they would in a conventional wildlife portrait.

Before taking the photograph, scan the entire outline. Check whether the animal’s legs are distinguishable, whether its head and ears are clearly defined, and whether important features are lost against nearby objects. With birds, pay particular attention to the wings and tail. A bird with its wings tucked tightly against its body may appear as a much simpler shape than one with its feathers spread.

Changing your position is often the easiest way to improve separation. Moving a short distance to one side can shift a branch out of the animal’s outline or create a gap between its legs. A lower shooting position may place the subject against the sky rather than vegetation, while a higher position can sometimes remove distracting foreground elements. These adjustments are especially useful in wetlands, grasslands, and wooded environments.

Multiple animals introduce another challenge. When individuals overlap, their silhouettes can merge into a single shape that is difficult to interpret. This does not mean you should always avoid groups. A group of birds in flight can create a compelling pattern, and animals gathered together may communicate social behavior. The important distinction is whether the arrangement remains visually understandable. Waiting for individuals to separate or for their positions to change can make the difference between a confusing cluster and a deliberate composition.

Exposing for a silhouette requires a different approach from a traditional wildlife portrait. Rather than preserving detail in the animal’s shadows, the goal is to retain important background information while letting the subject fall into darkness. This means exposing for the brighter surroundings instead of trying to balance the entire scene.

Automatic exposure modes can sometimes make this difficult. When a camera detects a large dark subject against a bright background, its metering system may attempt to brighten the scene. The result can be an animal with visible shadow detail instead of a solid silhouette. Exposure compensation provides a straightforward way to address this. Reducing exposure can keep the subject dark while preserving the sky’s colors and tonal information.

Manual exposure offers more control, particularly when the background brightness remains relatively consistent while the animal moves through the frame. You can establish an exposure based on the sky and maintain those settings rather than allowing the camera to continually adjust for changes in the composition. Spot or center-weighted metering can also help, depending on where you place the metering area and how your camera interprets the scene.

The histogram helps you evaluate exposure, especially when photographing colorful skies. Overexposing the brightest areas can remove the subtle color transitions that make the background interesting. Review the histogram and highlight warnings to determine whether you are retaining the tones you want. At the same time, don’t worry about preserving shadow detail in the animal if you intend to create a true silhouette.

Shutter speed remains important because wildlife behavior doesn’t become less unpredictable just because the subject is dark. A bird taking flight still needs a fast enough shutter speed to preserve the shape of its wings, and a running mammal may require a similarly fast exposure to prevent motion blur. If the animal is stationary, you may have more flexibility, but it is still worth accounting for small movements such as turning its head or shifting its weight.

Autofocus can become more challenging when the subject is dark against a bright background. Depending on the camera and scene, the autofocus system may have fewer visible details to identify. Tracking modes and subject detection can still help, but watch how reliably the camera follows the animal. In some situations, focusing on the subject before it moves into the brightest part of the background may be more effective. Continuous autofocus and burst shooting can help with unpredictable movement, but they work best when paired with an understanding of the animal’s likely path.

Although the animal itself is often rendered as a dark shape, the background can bring considerable color and atmosphere to a silhouette photograph. Sunrise and sunset provide familiar warm tones, but cooler twilight colors can work just as well. Deep blues, soft purples, and muted pastels can create a quieter mood, while reflections and layers of color can add depth without distracting from the subject.

Negative space gives the animal room to stand apart and allows the viewer to focus on its shape. This works especially well when photographing a small animal against a large sky or open landscape. The surrounding space becomes part of the story, communicating scale and emphasizing how the subject fits into its environment.

Minimalist compositions often work well because they reduce competing elements. A single bird against a colorful sky, an elk standing on a distant ridge, or a fox crossing an open field can create a strong image with very little visual information. However, minimalism does not mean every photograph needs only one subject. A small number of carefully arranged elements can create balance, rhythm, or visual contrast.

Reflections offer another way to add visual interest while keeping the composition simple. A bird standing in shallow water may produce a second shape beneath its body, creating symmetry or a repeating pattern. A calm lake can also provide a contrasting surface, depending on the direction of the light. These compositions can be particularly effective when the reflection remains recognizable and adds something to the overall arrangement.

Another way to use minimalism is to move in closer and create a tighter portrait, emphasizing the animal’s outline and the details that define its shape. At this distance, subtle textures and contours become more prominent, adding visual interest while keeping the composition simple. This is another time when I play with my exposure to decide if I want a flat silhouette or one with more information in the darkened areas.

Silhouettes, or backlit images, aren’t always the best approach for every wildlife encounter. Many situations require an animal’s coloration, markings, expression, or visible behavior to tell the story. A close portrait that reveals the texture of fur or the details of a bird’s plumage may communicate far more than a dark outline. Deciding whether to photograph a subject as a silhouette should come down to what the image is meant to convey.

When shape or gesture is the most interesting part of the scene, removing detail can strengthen the photograph. A bird spreading its wings against a sunset, an elk calling from a ridgeline, or a mammal looking toward an open horizon can communicate its presence through posture alone. The viewer does not need to see every detail to understand the moment. Instead, the simplified form encourages them to focus on the animal’s movement and relationship with the environment.

Most of all, silhouettes can add variety to a wildlife portfolio. Photographers naturally spend considerable time pursuing sharp, detailed images, particularly when working with long telephoto lenses and tracking fast-moving subjects. A silhouette offers a different visual approach, emphasizing composition and light over revealing every feature. It can help tell a broader story about an encounter or location, especially when paired with more traditional wildlife portraits.

When conditions allow, photograph a scene both ways. A traditional exposure may reveal the animal’s markings and expression, while a silhouette may create a more graphic, atmospheric interpretation of the same moment. Comparing the two approaches can help you decide which communicates the scene most effectively.

Ultimately, wildlife silhouette photography is about recognizing the visual strength of an animal’s shape. Distinctive anatomy, expressive posture, thoughtful composition, and suitable light all contribute to an image that remains compelling without the details normally associated with wildlife photography. Sometimes, revealing less about an animal allows its shape, movement, and place in the landscape to tell a more compelling story.

#9181. Solid cork forms walls of pavilion dedicated to silence at Casa No Tempo in Alentejo

Photography by Mercês Tomaz Gomes

Antwerp-based studio Corkinho has unveiled its latest “still room”, a pavilion with walls of solid cork, which is installed in the grounds of a vacation villa designed by Manuel Aires Mateus.

The still room is a space dedicated to silent and introspective activities, such as reading, yoga, tea ceremonies or meditation.

Corkinho installed it in the grounds of Casa No Tempo, a former farmhouse in southern Portugal, which architect Aires Mateus converted into a holiday home in 2014 for hospitality entrepreneur João Rodrigues.

Lead designer Cédric Etienne devised the building’s innovative structure, which is fully demountable, with the help of architect and master carpenter Gonçalo Madeira Marrote of Madeiguincho.

The floor slab is a timber deck, built over a foundation of removable concrete blocks.

Above this, solid blocks of cork are stacked up like giant bricks to form the building’s walls and secured with metal rods that thread through milled channels.

The pavilion is topped by a timber roof, described by Etienne as “like a hat with four screws”, which helps to weigh down the cork blocks.

“I wanted it to be zero waste and carbon-neutral,” the designer told Dezeen.

“If we need to dismantle it, we can place it somewhere else. There is no glue and no screws,” he said.

“It’s like the Japanese way of building teahouses, with total respect of the local materials and no harm to the land.”

As the name suggests, Corkinho is a studio that specialises in objects and spaces built from cork.

The studio first launched the still room concept in 2020, when it moved its office into the former Noorderpershuis power station in Antwerp and transformed one of the rooms into a silent sanctuary.

Etienne defines a still room as any space where you can pause your mind and be still.

“It’s a place where you disconnect from noise and distractions and invite a deeper sense of presence,” he said.

After consulting with various hotel brands keen to adopt the concept, Etienne pitched the idea to Rodrigues and his company, Silent Living.

The company has five properties, all designed by Aires Mateus and all with a focus on slow living.

“I had been to Casa No Tempo many times, so I knew the place like an inner home,” the designer said.

“It felt so aligned in terms of feeling and senses, so I thought it could be a really beautiful challenge to move the concept forward in this place,” he continued.

The room can be used by guests staying at the villa, but it can also accommodate curated programmes.

Etienne has been hosting four-day silent retreats, allowing groups of designers and hospitality professionals to learn more about the still room concept.

The cork blocks, supplied by locally based company Sofalca, were heat-treated to improve their durability. The material gives the building impressive sensorial and thermal qualities, Etienne said.

“All the technical properties of cork – the acoustics, the scent, the softness – all become architectural conditions,” he stated.

“You really feel like you’re coming into a womb. Even when it’s 40 degrees outside, the temperature inside is around 22 or 23.”

Other pavilions recently featured in Dezeen include a wildlife pavilion informed by rippling water and a jigsaw-like pavilion made of mass-timber scrap.

Photography by Mercês Tomaz Gomes

#9179. Samyang AF 60-180mm f/2.8 Review: A Trinity Completed

Samyang AF 60-180mm f/2.8 Review: A Trinity Completed

The two major third-party manufacturers from Japan have a complete trinity of full-frame professional f/2.8 zoom lenses. Sigma has long had a complete set, and Tamron has its excellent G2 series finalized. The Chinese companies are only now venturing into the autofocusing pro zoom lens market, but Samyang, out of Korea, has worked very hard — and quickly — to complete its full set, too. With the release of the new $1,099 Samyang X Schneider Kreuznach AF 60-180mm f/2.8, that goal is realized.This lens has some surprises up its sleeve, but the experience still feels lacking in features and refinement. PetaPixel Score 7/10 ProsVery sharp right to the cornersLightweight and compactBokeh has a pleasing rendering of backgroundsConsButtons and controls feel down-marketBasic and slower stepping autofocus motorNo optical stabilizationNo aperture ring This lens is being released for E-mount and L-mount cameras, and whether you should buy it will be highly dependent on that lens mount.

This lens has some surprises up its sleeve, but the experience still feels lacking in features and refinement.

I’m going to get this out of the way first: Samyang lenses, also sold under the Rokinon brand in North America, have always aimed at a budget price point and, as a result, rely heavily on plastic construction. Okay, lots of companies do, but Samyang lenses always just look and feel a little less refined and a little more basic than some of the others.

I’m not going to go so far as to say that this negatively impacts the build quality. I know many Rokinon users who have had years of reliable service out of their lenses. But the buttons and controls always feel a little flimsy and make obtrusive clicking noises when pressed. The plastic hood is basic and twists into place with a little bit of coercion.

The rubber rings feature two different textures, which Samyang usually likes to use. There is a custom button and an AF/MF switch, along with an unexpected locking switch for the zoom mechanism. The manual focus ring has a nice smoothness to it, but the zoom ring takes a bit of force to get moving and lacks refinement.

Flicking this will keep the zoom at the 60mm mark, but you do have to unlock it before zooming again. You will not find an aperture ring on this lens, but this is pretty standard at this price point. Samyang lenses do have some baffles and a little weather sealing incorporated into the lens mount.

With the 77mm filter threads on the front, this lens looks fairly hefty, but with an overall weight of 730 grams, it is actually lighter than the Tamron and Sigma alternatives. I also like that the lens doesn’t extend that far when zoomed to 180mm, and the point of balance doesn’t change much either. However, part of the lighter weight comes with a lack of optical image stabilization within the lens.

I was worried about the bokeh on this lens when I started with specular highlight tests. At the widest apertures, the highlights have a truncated look, which I do not prefer, and there are some slight onion rings present as well. However, at tighter apertures, the highlights are fairly round, and more importantly, the actual rendering of the out-of-focus areas of the images is quite smooth. I expected a harsher edge to the bokeh with a more distracting rendering, but the backgrounds looked soft and pleasant. Other than the distracting highlights, this lens presents shallow depth of field beautifully.

There is a little bit of flare present, which is something I found with the other Samyang f/2.8 lenses. At f/2.8, there is some green ghosting and a bit of veiled flare washing out the image. The green cast stays at tighter apertures but doesn’t get too obnoxious. Overall, the flare control is decent, and the hood will do a good job of blocking extraneous light. Speaking of color casts, expect a little bit of LoCA at the wider apertures. These longitudinal chromatic aberrations will present with a slight green and magenta split, but the effect is minimal and usually won’t cause much concern in the vast majority of your images.

Sharpness is where this lens excels, with excellent detail in the center of the image right from the start. I found the 180mm mark to be particularly good in the center at f/2.8, with slight improvement to be found at tighter apertures. The corners at the long end were also impressive, with more detail than I expected at f/2.8 and fairly low vignetting. Closing the aperture will improve things as usual, but I was impressed by how good the corner detail was overall. At the 60mm mark, the story is similar. The center sharpness is maybe slightly softer at this focal length, but still very acceptable. The corners were also similarly excellent, with far better-than-expected detail. This Samyang lens has the most consistent corners and overall detail compared to its third-party contemporaries.

The lack of lens-based image stabilization is unfortunate, although to be fair, the impact will largely depend on what camera body you are using. Clearly, the lack of a stabilizer keeps the cost down a bit and shaves off some weight. Another cost-cutting choice is the use of a more basic stepping motor for focus. Focusing is smooth and accurate, but the speed is noticeably slower than the competition. If you want to tackle faster sports and action, you might want to consider alternatives.

Kudos to Samyang for finalizing a trilogy of professional-grade f/2.8 full-frame zoom lenses. However, should you buy this set or even any of these lenses individually? Here is what we can say for certain: in my opinion, Samyang lenses are well-built but lack refinement, and tend to lack extra controls and aperture rings.

They always feel a little down-market in the hand to me, but the optical performance is formidable. This 60-180mm f/2.8 is both compact and frighteningly sharp. Its optical performance beyond that is certainly acceptable, but it doesn’t ever seem to shine in any other regard. Samyang has a 14-24mm and 24-60mm lens, both with f/2.8 apertures, and they are both capable of capturing great images. However, in a field of fierce competition, Samyang lenses may struggle to find a foothold.

Samyang AF 14-24mm f/2.8Buy new on B&HSamyang AF 14-24mm f/2.8Buy used on KEH.comSamyang AF 24-60mm f/2.8Buy new on B&HSamyang AF 24-60mm f/2.8Buy used on KEH.com

In Sony E-mount, this 60-180mm lens goes up against the Tamron 70-180mm f/2.8 Di III VC VXD G2, which almost exactly matches the $1,099 Samyang.

In L-mount, it only has to compete with the Sigma 70-200mm f/2.8 Sports and Panasonic S 70-200mm f/2.8, both of which are much larger and more expensive options. I’d probably go for the Tamron 70-180mm f/2.8 myself due to the faster AF experience and optical stabilization. However, if you value maximum sharpness and slightly less weight, and have a camera body with IBIS, or if you are looking for an excellent option in L-mount, the Samyang 60-180mm could be a sound choice.

Sigma 70-200mm f/2.8 SportsBuy new on B&HSigma 70-200mm f/2.8 SportsBuy used on KEH.comPanasonic Lumix S 70-200mm f/2.8Buy new on B&HPanasonic Lumix S 70-200mm f/2.8Buy used on KEH.com

Regardless of lens mount, the Sigma 70-200mm f/2.8 Sports is going to be much larger at a higher cost, and only makes sense if you want to use teleconverters. This is pretty much the same story for the Panasonic S 70-200mm f/2.8 as well. The Tamron does offer similar optical performance with better AF and stabilization, and is even more compact and manageable. The Samyang 60-180mm should put pressure on Sigma to make a better alternative, but Tamron has nothing to worry about.

Yes. This lens is still going to deliver excellent images at a good price and in a compact chassis. Whichever way you slice it, the Samyang is still a good tool for the dollar.

#9178. One museum visit a month could improve health, new report finds

The author Daisy Fancourt and Jenny Waldman, the Art Fund's director, view the ‘Recommended Dose of Art: A Prescription for Health and Wellbeing’ report at London’s Wallace Collection

David Parry/Assignments/Press Association

Visiting a museum or art gallery for just one hour a month could significantly improve people's physical and mental health, according to a new report which calls for cultural engagement to become as routine as exercise and healthy eating.

The research, commissioned by the charity Art Fund in partnership with University College London professor Daisy Fancourt, recommends that people spend at least 60 minutes with art in museums and galleries every month.

However, the survey of 2,000 UK adults found that 89% fail to meet this proposed target, equivalent to an estimated 49.5 million people.

The report, “The Recommended Dose of Art: A Prescription for Health and Wellbeing”, draws together scientific evidence suggesting that regular cultural engagement can reduce stress, improve cognitive health and potentially extend life expectancy.

Previous studies have shown that regular museum and gallery visits could nearly halve the risk of developing depression over the following decade. Other studies have linked cultural participation with reduced dementia risk and lower levels of loneliness.

Viewing original artworks in galleries was also associated with a 22% greater reduction in the stress hormone cortisol compared with viewing reproductions.

Fancourt, whose book Art Cure on the scientific benefits of art came out earlier this year, says regular engagement with art should be considered a health-promoting behaviour alongside exercise, a balanced diet and spending time outdoors.

“Guidelines like eating our 5-a-day of fruit and vegetables and getting our 10,000 steps have proven effective in helping us to prioritise other health-promoting behaviours in our busy lives,” she says in a statement. “Adding regular arts engagement to this list could be a simple and joyful way of investing further in our health and wellbeing.”

But the findings also raise questions about whether Britain's struggling museums have the resources to encourage more frequent visits. Jenny Waldman, the director of Art Fund, tells The Art Newspaper that the research strengthens the case for sustained public investment in museums, including protecting free admission at national institutions and supporting local and regional collections.

“We want to see sustained, long-term public investment across the museum sector, so that all museums have the resources to care for their collections and welcome the widest possible audiences,” she says.

Waldman acknowledged that removing admission charges alone would not overcome barriers to visiting museums, including accessibility and the resources available to institutions.

She says Art Fund's research among museum directors found that 36% of museums had reduced their opening hours because of insufficient funding and staffing.

“If we want museums to play a greater role in supporting public health, we must invest in the sector and give them the means to do so,” she adds.

Waldman also points to international developments, including Greece's introduction of arts prescribing into its national healthcare system and growing recognition of cultural organisations as public health assets. She also notes efforts closer to home: “Scotland's Chief Medical Officer, Sir Gregor Smith, recently published a report recognising arts organisations as important public health assets and calling for arts and culture to be embedded more widely in Scotland's approach to public health.”

The Cardiff museum is the first Welsh winner of the £100,000 prize, beating other finalists including V&A Dundee and Pitt Rivers Museum

The approximately $9m project included modernising 20,000 sq. ft of galleries and bringing key objects out of storage for public display for the first time

The museum has been praised for the ambitious way it has shared its collections and for its social outreach

#9177. Many London architecture firms not paying London Living Wage

The majority of the London-based studios in The Pay 100‘s fifth annual salary survey are not paying Part I architectural assistants the London Living Wage, as required by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA).

An engineering firm has topped the leaderboard for the average salaries for UK architects, according to a survey conducted by the anonymous group The Pay 100.

Engineering firm tops architect salary leaderboard

Published over the weekend, the survey provides rough figures only based on the mean figures submitted by respondents. This year’s data collected the annual salary of 127 firms in the UK and the mean number of hours of unpaid overtime per week.

Topping the leaderboard with the highest average annual salary for architects with less than five years’ experience is BakerHicks, an engineering and design firm, which paid £72,000, according to the survey.

Second on the list is London studio Hawkins\Brown at £63,700, and joint third at £56,300 are London practices Samuel Chisholm Studio and Thomas Alexander Design.

The survey also presented figures for Part I and Part II architectural assistants. Transport for London had the highest wage for Part II roles at £44,000, followed by Foster + Partners at £42,000.

Majority of London firms not paying London Living Wage

The results for Part I roles included salaries from 30 studios, 21 of which were based in Greater London.

Only the top four studios on the leaderboard – Haworth Tompkins, Allford Hall Monaghan Morris, Studio McW and Studio PDP – paid more than the London Living Wage of £32,136, which RIBA declared a requirement for relevant offices.

Twelve of the 30 studios were paying Part I roles less than the £29,328 UK Living Wage.

Low wages “a threat to the future of the profession”

Alongside its survey data, The Pay 100 wrote an open letter to RIBA, asking it to take action on the financial wellbeing of those working in the architecture industry and to ensure the long-term future of the profession.

“Our aim has always been to create tangible financial incentives for employers to improve pay, empower employees to make informed career decisions, and encourage a healthier, more sustainable profession,” said The Pay 100 in the letter.

“We recognise that architecture practices operate within a highly competitive market, often under significant financial pressure themselves,” it continued. “Nevertheless, the commercial challenges facing practices should not prevent the profession from addressing the deteriorating conditions experienced by many employees.”

“Poor financial conditions for staff are not merely an employment issue; they are a threat to the long-term health, resilience and future of the profession.”

It went on to set out two courses of action it called for RIBA to take: establishing “meaningful minimum salaries” for RIBA chartered practices, and taking full ownership of The Pay 100 and its annual salary survey.

The Pay 100 said a framework of minimum salary levels should be established across different architecture roles, increasing year-on-year in line with inflation.

“A profession cannot sustainably advocate for the value of its services while leaving the financial conditions of its workforce to market pressures alone,” it said. “The RIBA should take a leading role in addressing this imbalance.”

After five years of aiming to improve pay transparency with its annual surveys, The Pay 100 wants RIBA to take ownership of the survey and commit resources to it, developing it into an industry-wide initiative.

“We believe that improving pay transparency across UK architecture should be a core responsibility of the profession’s leading membership body,” said The Pay 100.

“Under the RIBA’s stewardship, the survey could benefit from significantly greater reach, sustained institutional support and broader participation across the profession,” it continued.

“This would provide a foundation for more comprehensive salary data, stronger engagement between employers and employees, and meaningful progress towards better financial conditions throughout the industry.”

The Pay 100 ended its letter by asking for a public response from RIBA by 1 December

#9175. Brick bathhouse by Kengo Kuma nears completion in Copenhagen

Pyramidal towers frame pools at the Kai Water Culture House by Japanese studio Kengo Kuma & Associates, which is nearing completion in Copenhagen.

Set to open on the city’s harbour in December, the 5,800-square-metre aquatic centre will contain ten indoor and outdoor pools, alongside wellness facilities and cultural spaces.

Kengo Kuma & Associates was commissioned alongside Danish firms Cornelius Vöge, Søren Jensen and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects to realise the new cultural and recreational facility on the city’s artificial island of Christiansholm – known locally as Papirøen, or Paper Island.

Photos revealed ahead of the opening show the facility’s five staggered buildings perched atop a glazed base and fronted by a wooden pier that provides direct access to the sea.

“The Water Culture House is a significant new landmark on Copenhagen’s waterfront,” Kengo Kuma & Associates lead architect Yuki Ikeguchi said. “It is part of the story of the city and the harbour’s transformation from an industrial to a cultural harbour.”

“As the cultural cornerstone of Papirøen, the house is a gathering place with water and community as its focal point, embraced by a public harbour bath,” Ikeguchi added.

Constructed from 300,000 handmade bricks, the tapered volumes are punctuated by triangular and square openings that filter dappled light into the indoor pools.

“The bricks are arranged in a staggered, stepped pattern, giving the building its distinctive texture and sculptural character,” Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects said.

“A total of 403 windows of varying sizes act as viewing apertures, framing the surroundings and creating captivating experiences of natural light as it shifts throughout the day,” it added.

The tallest of the five volumes, dubbed the Culture Tower, houses the centre’s cultural programmes, which include a third-floor events space. Meanwhile, the other four towers each house lofty indoor pools.

Nestled between the five brick volumes on the first floor is an outdoor pool, framed by the building’s sloped facades, and an open-air Onsen – a Japanese-style hot spring – that overlooks the harbour.

The Kai Water Culture House is set to open to the public on 5 December, with its wooden pier slated for completion early next year.

The facility sits among a wider redevelopment of Copenhagen’s Paper Island led by Danish studio COBE. Recent projects on the island include a 20,000-square-metre apartment complex informed by the area’s 300-year-old warehouses.

#9174. Nuart Aberdeen 2026: Poetry In The Streets

Welcome to the latest edition of Nuart Aberdeen. As far as we can ascertain, this will be the first street art festival in the world with a focus primarily on poetry and text-based works. Over the years, for better or worse, the large scale colourful figurative mural has come to dominate the culture we work with, and although it’s an aspect of the culture we support, due to the resources required to produce murals, they’re perhaps also the least democratic form of art on the streets. As curators, researchers and producers working in “festival” culture, we have a responsibility to not only showcase and celebrate the most interesting and technically competent works of our time, but to also ensure the culture’s development and survival. The only way to do this, is to inspire and encourage those without the privilege of a fine art degree or access to the arts, to have a go themselves. This has always been Nuart’s primary goal, not just to produce art, but to also inspire and produce the next generation of artists. A lofty goal, particularly as it’s often in conflict with the stated needs of sponsors and partners, on paper at least, and no one stands in front of a Tower block mural and thinks, I’ll pop home and have a go myself on the gable end of Gran’s house.

What we do have evidence for, is that the smaller, more human scale works – the stencils and paste ups and interventions – do have this effect. You could say that the ease of copying a Banksy stencil, which requires no more than a craft knife, a piece of cardboard and an idea, is the very foundation of this culture. We’ve seen this happen time and time again. Indeed, several of the producers and artists joining us this year, started their artistic journey as assistants and volunteers at Nuart.

At Nuart, we’ve always prided ourselves on not only showcasing the BIG names in muralism, but on also using the festival as a place to explore and experiment with new forms and ideas that engage with the idea of the whole city as a canvas, and not just the wall. In this respect, Nuart Aberdeen have been fortunate enough to have the support of some of the most thoughtful and progressive partners that an event such as Nuart could possibly have, and this year is no different.

Whilst pondering this issue, how to balance the needs of partners, tourist boards, with the need to impress the public, and create works of curiosity and interest for scholars which inspire the next generation, I imagined a city without art on the streets, with no forms of public expression, where all art is concealed behind the walls of city institutions and under guard 24/7. And then I recalled a piece of graffiti sprayed on the walls of Paris during the 1968 student uprising, an event which saw waves of creative energy explode onto the streets. It read, “La poésie est dans la rue”, or “Poetry is in the Streets” – could we harness some of this energy at Nuart to revitalise and energise the culture?

A short while later, I remembered a quote from pioneering UK graffiti writer Mode2. He was discussing how graffiti culture had taken hold and blossomed in the UK in the 1980s, and in a throwaway quip had said, the reason it took hold was because regardless of how interested you were in making art at school, if you couldn’t draw or paint realistically, you were bottom of the class. Then graffiti came along, and it struck everyone that all you had to know to create and engage with it, was your ABC’s.

And that was it. It was these two quite innocuous events that formed the genesis of this year’s poetry and text based Nuart. These are forms of creative expression that we all have access to and I hope the festival sparks the public’s imagination in the same way that those early bubble letters and Banksy stencils did.

Thank you as ever to all of our sponsors, partners and to the city council, for allowing us once again to make a contribution to what we believe is a magical and inspiring city.

— Martyn Reed, Nuart Founder and CuratorArtists include: Alisa Oleva (UK) Ciarán Glöbel (SCT) dr.d AKA Subvertiser (UK) HICKS (UK) James Klinge (SCT) KMG (SCT) Molly Hankinson (UK) Remi Rough (UK) Robert Montgomery (SCT) The Rebel Bear (SCT) The Writing Is On The Wall (UK) Trackie McLeod (SCT)  V2k | (LT - SCT)

#9173. Paul Hamlyn Foundation announces recipients of £75,000 Awards for Artists

Award winners left to right: Hayley Tompkins, Daudi Matsiko, Bushra El-Turk, Linda Bell, Olivia Chaney, Rory Pilgrim, Ayanna Witter-Johnson, Georgina Starr, Charlotte Keeffe, (Racheal Crowther not present).Photo credit: Emile Holba

The Turner prize nominee Rory Pilgrim and the Venice Biennale artist Hayley Tompkins are among the recipients of this year’s Paul Hamlyn Foundation’s Awards for Artists. The £75,000 awards were granted to five artists and five composers.

In the wake of the ongoing cost of living crisis, the awards are timely. “Unique in its no-strings-attached funding model, the [Hamlyn] awards for artists allows recipients to use their award as they wish, providing them the freedom to develop their creative ideas, alleviating the pressures they may be facing,” says a press statement.

Tompkins was part of a trio of artists, alongside Corin Sworn and Duncan Campbell, who showed works in the Scotland + Venice exhibition in 2013. Her installations combine painting with a variety of other media, including found objects, digital films, photography and furniture. “It still hasn’t felt real yet, but I do know with more resources there will be room for me to feel and move a bit differently now,” she says in a statement.

Pilgrim’s work explores how “activism, spirituality and music can create spaces for connection”, adds the statement. Bristol-born Pilgrim was nominated for the Turner Prize in 2023 for their commission RAFTS at Serpentine Galleries and Barking Town Hall. “After working on many intensive processes, [the award] gives invaluable breathing space, autonomy and financial security to find joy and excitement in creativity,” Pilgrim says.

The other successful artists this year are Georgina Starr, who is known for performance works such as Androgynous Egg (2017), Dublin-born artist Racheal Crowther and the learning disabled artist Linda Bell. Judges include Joe Hill, the director of Yorkshire Sculpture Park, Melissa Blanchflower, a senior curator at Turner Contemporary in Margate, and Sheryll Catto, the artistic director of ActionSpace.

Since 1994, Paul Hamlyn Foundation has made 377 awards to artists with over £12m in funding; Phyllida Barlow, Yinka Shonibare and Alberta Whittle are among the previous recipients. Five composers including Daudi Matsiko and Ayanna Witter-Johnson were also recognised.

#9172. Cinga Samson "Ukuphuthelwa" @ White Cube Gallery, NYC

South African artist Cinga Samson’s exhibition of new paintings is titled ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, an isiXhosa word in the artist’s native language that translates as ‘unable to sleep’. Unlike the English word ‘insomnia’, the isiXhosa term carries no negative connotation and accordingly, for Samson, sleeplessness is not a condition to be cured but a state of spiritual alertness, a sensitivity that deepens in the dark. Rendered in the artist’s signature occluded palette of near-blacks, carbon and deep Prussian blues, Samson’s scenes depict men-like figures, dogs in overgrown fields and portraits of plant life native to South Africa. Encouraging slow, contemplative looking, a sense of existential gravity pervades Samson’s new series of oil paintings, attempting to depict a vast reality that is continuously in motion. As the artist has it, his quandary pertains to the existential question of how to create a ‘true and honest painting'. The exhibition will be on view through April 18, 2026.

With ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, Samson considers his role as an artist in relation to his inability to represent the whole truth of reality, and the fact that he can merely make symbols. Between the static, painted sign and the fluid experience it gestures towards, he contends that there exists a gulf that no image can close. Though the technical mastery and convincing realism of these paintings appear to invite interpretation, the artist asserts that his work confronts the very dilemma of representation: that the image can only ever be a relative symbol of what it reflects, never its equivalent. Acknowledging the open-ended nature of symbols and their subjective interpretation, Samson takes the figure of the dog as an example. The viewer may, for instance, look at Intsingiselo II (2026) and perceive the loyalty conventionally associated with dogs, while an amaXhosa understanding might highlight the dog as signifying the guiding, protective principles of ancestors. Comprising painstaking detail and deft brushwork, Samson’s paintings do not disguise the limits of representation but, rather, aspire to harness his skills towards that which exceeds the representable. Above all, the artist’s work seeks out the authority of the unnameable and the territory of the sublime, one in which the divine is not found elsewhere but present in the vernacular of all things.

Samson’s larger compositions carry a palpable sense of reverence and ceremony. In Umlindo (Watcher) (2026), figures are gathered in a forest clearing with wildflower bouquets and lengths of fabric, a scene that carries the visual grammar of ritual without specifying its addressee or terms. For Samson however, ‘the ritual itself is not the important thing – it’s an opening to what exists beyond’, and the paintings use the aesthetics of ritual to speak to a collective need for orientation, as well as the capacity of ritual to mediate an encounter with a vast unknown. That the works are titled with enigmatic words and phrases in isiXhosa, such as Imfihlo (Secret) and Intsingiselo (Meaning) (both 2026), infer the same problem the paintings contend with – the instability of interpretation as it pertains to the knowable and unknowable. Each word carries a weight in isiXhosa that its English translation approaches but can never fully reach; here, just as between the painted sign and living referent, meaning slips between the interstice of two languages.

The objects, people and settings that recur in these paintings and across Samson’s oeuvre are identifiable and quotidian, yet Samson corrals in each an unexplained mystery. In Tshee (2026), a vast field stretches out, the silhouetted trees meeting a murky sky, though the void of the night is interrupted by a moonwashed cloud, its brilliant white destabilising the eerie, cold atmosphere suffused with majesty. ‘The sky can be so friendly, but sometimes so heavy, dark, so scary. It’s the same energy, but it exists in different forms’, Samson notes, conjuring an oscillation between the approachable and the overwhelming that recalls the affective register of the sublime. Sithini ngelilitye (2026), distils the same sensation: a rocky crag emerges from arid undergrowth, its surface rendered in forensic detail against a sky of barely-there wash, charging the scene with the same quality of mute enormity.

Marshalling light ‘like a magic trick’, Samson imparts a unique kind of rhythm to his paintings – a flickering that emerges and disperses across the picture plane, granting varying degrees of visibility to the dark, nighttime scenes. Producing an unsteadiness that is at once optical and psychical, the artist leaves large sections of the painting’s under-drawing visible to lend moments of transparency to the work. In Isiganeko (2026), for example, thin layers of glaze are applied and wiped back in his typical style, a means of building colour that lends the figures a brooding chromatic density, whilst elsewhere, in the undergrowth and the bird caught mid-flight, the under-drawing is left entirely exposed. In all Samson’s figures, the pupils of the eyes are left unpainted and allow ‘light’ to further circulate, a decision that renders them porous, so they are ‘completely one with the whole painting’. Without pupils, these figures are not personified identities, but ‘human’ forms enmeshed with the painting’s landscape and atmosphere, no element ever possessing full mastery over the other. In places where the ‘trick’ of painting reveals itself, it is as if Samson’s works were stepping back from the pretence or promise of representation. What ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ reaches towards is not individual transcendence in subordination, but rather the mystery that can be unearthed in ordinary forms, whose immanent magic is available to those who are sensitive to it. This is the condition that ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ ultimately describes: not an absence or deficit, but a hypersensitivity that affords everything in existence the same potential for eliciting wonder or fear. Samson’s pupilless figures do not ‘look’ outward because the figures’ knowing comes from within the world they inhabit, a shared knowledge that exists between the bowing foliage, the vigilant dog, the bird in flight and the foreboding of the night sky enshrouding them all. In Samson’s hands, each optical device and representational motif prises apart what it cannot contain, in service of painting ‘a thing that links us to God – by God, I mean everything’.

Malika Favre and Kumkum Fernando blend music, mythology and '60s flower power.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Forty years ago, Montreux Jazz Festival brought together the great US pop artists Andy Warhol and Keith Haring to create the poster design for the annual event. The result was a vibrant fusion of styles celebrating jazz music and rhythm. Now, the festival has repeated the experiment for just a second time, uniting two acclaimed contemporary artists for a dream collaboration.

The 2027 poster design was created by the French illustrator Malika Favre and the Sri Lankan sculptural artist and designer Kumkum Fernando. The former's distinctive geometric graphic style merges with the latter's colourful retrofuturism in a striking maximalist design that channels diverse influences into the form of a divine being that represents music as a joyful, spiritual journey.

Montreux has a long history of artist-designed posters. Other previous contributors have included David Bowie, Jean Tinguely, Yoann Lemoine (Woodkid), Lakwena, Kévin Germanier and Christian Marclay.

Keith Haring designed for the festival twice. For his second commission, in 1986, he worked with Andy Warhol as a collaborator. The festival invited Malika to adopt a similar approach for her second contribution, ten years after her first design for Montreux.

While her 2017 poster stood out for its minimalism, the new design goes in the opposite direction. A densely packed arrangement of colour and shapes creates a fantastical figure that looks like a cross between a robot, sacred altar and a jukebox. In fact, the design is also being turned into a sculptural vinyl cabinet (see further below).

“I fell in love with the festival on my very first visit in 2017. The poster I created for that edition remains one of my personal favourites to this day. I knew it would be hard to match, so I wanted to take the opposite approach: to create a work bursting with colour, as maximalist as the first one was minimalist. Kumkum was the ideal artist for this,” Favre says of the collaboration.

The design draws on diverse influences, including South Asian traditions, retro-futurism and '60s counterculture. The flowers evoke the lakeside quays of Montreux but also the flower power movement of the hippie era, a nod to the fact that Montreux Jazz Festival was founded during the 1967 Summer of Love. The floral patterns also subtly outline lips, kisses and female faces – symbols of love, pleasure and sexuality that recur throughout Malika's artistic universe.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

“I had this vision of music blooming in Montreux, this feeling of the entire town coming alive during the festival,” Favre adds. “I wanted to convey that joy. The world is going through strange times, and a festival like Montreux is an opportunity to celebrate. For me, flowers also symbolise eroticism, an explosion of the senses and the pleasures found in music. I always like to tuck in something a little cheeky, and I thought I could bring that touch of a feminine sensuality. When I sent the first flowers to Kumkum he said, ‘Oh yes, that’s sexy!’”

From the outset, the idea was also to bring the poster’s divine entity into the world as a three-dimensional object, following Kumkum’s practice of creating futuristic, geometric sculptures. The result is a made-for-order vinyl cabinet with a dedicated turntable compartment and pull-out drawers for record storage.

“The spark came when we noticed the resemblance between the shape of certain religious altars and that of a jukebox, both sharing the same sense of symmetry,” Fernando says. “We imagined a kind of gateway into a sacred realm of music, a timeless entity, part retro-futuristic robot, part mythological being, that embodies music as a joyful, universal experience.”

The 61st Montreux Jazz Festival will take place on the Lake Geneva shoreline from 2 July to 17 July 2027.

#9170. Jaguar designs Knightsbridge flagship to be "physical expression" of Type 01 electric car

Photography courtesy of Jaguar Land Rover

British car brand Jaguar has redesigned its flagship store in Knightsbridge, London, which is the only place in the world where the public can see the recently unveiled Type 01 electric car.

Jaguar overhauled itp show in central London to align its aesthetic with its latest electric car, which was created as the first car in a new era for the brand. It aimed for the flagship store to be a clear departure from the traditional car showroom.

“[We wanted] to create a physical expression of the new Jaguar,” said Jaguar Land Rover spatial brand design team senior manager Nick Rolls, whose team was responsible for overhauling the store.

“Rather than a traditional showroom, we wanted to design a destination where architecture, culture, hospitality and craftsmanship come together – and London felt like a natural home for that vision,” he continued.

“The space has been purpose-designed from the ground up to embody the brand’s new identity – it gave us the opportunity to truly rethink what a Jaguar destination could be outside traditional conventions.”

The showroom has space for two cars to be displayed, one of which is currently the Type 01, with the showroom being the only place in the world where it is on display to the public.

However, the majority of the ground floor of the space is occupied by a restaurant.

Named Café Eighty-One, the restaurant by Michelin-starred chef Michael O’Hare was finished in rich red fabric.

Upholstered benches run around the space, while a series of booths line the front facade of the showroom.

“Food is one of the most universal forms of connection,” said Rolls. “We wanted Café Eighty-One to be a welcoming space where people could spend time, meet friends or discover something new.

“It’s designed to be a destination in its own right, helping make Jaguar at Knightsbridge part of London’s cultural and hospitality landscape,” he continued.

According to Rolls, the extensive use of red was a nod to the surrounding brick architecture in central London.

“Jaguar’s design philosophy is exuberant modernism, so colour plays an important role in creating emotion, atmosphere and a sense of occasion,” he said.

“The rich reds within Café Eighty-One were inspired by London’s iconic red-brick architecture, which is so prevalent throughout Knightsbridge and the surrounding neighbourhoods,” he continued. “It was a way of connecting the interior to its setting while creating a warm, vibrant environment that feels distinctly London.”

Through the rest of the spaces, the materials and colours were chosen to directly evoke the interiors of the Type 01 electric car.

“The relationship is deliberate,” said Rolls. “The interiors share the same emphasis on materiality, craftsmanship and bold, contemporary form that defines Type 01.”

“Materials such as travertine, tactile textiles and warm brass reference the vehicle’s interior, while the use of sculptural shapes, carefully composed lighting and strong geometric forms reflects the same creative philosophy behind the car,” he continued.

While the public restaurant and showroom space are on the ground floor, a lower level contains more private spaces for sales, meetings and for discussions about customisation.

One of these, called the Design Vault, was entirely finished in rich navy blues.

Overall, Rolls hopes that the revamped space will help people understand the current, major rethink that the brand is embarking on.

“I hope people leave with a deeper understanding of Jaguar,” he concluded.

“Every element of the destination has been designed to reflect craftsmanship, creativity and bold design. We want people to feel a genuine connection to the brand and to see Jaguar through a new lens.”

The creation of the showroom follows the launch of Jaguar’s second electric car earlier this year, the Type 01. The car is the production version of the much-discussed Type 00 concept car, which drew much attention in 2024 when it was unveiled following a rebrand for the car company, which was described as a “complete reset”.

#9169. Sophia Huitema "Prussian Blue" @ Harper’s Apartment

Harper’s is pleased to announce Prussian Blue, New York–based artist Sophia Huitema’s first solo exhibition with the gallery. The presentation features new works by Huitema and will be on view through April 25, 2026.

Across the seven oil paintings on view, the visual and chemical properties of the pigment Prussian Blue function as a metaphorical anchor, tying together a cast of watchful female figures within Huitema’s hazy, dreamlike worlds. Working within a restrained range of blue and green tones, the paintings evoke a moody atmosphere through cool harmonies and dimly lit interiors. Prussian Blue, derived from chemical processes historically linked to cyanide while also used as an antidote to certain forms of poisoning, embodies a rare duality in which toxicity and protection converge, mirroring the emotionally guarded, ambiguous presence of Huitema’s figures.

The tension between beauty and menace permeates Huitema’s subjects. Elongated figures with exaggerated limbs and slender necks slink through each scene, often directly confronting the viewer’s gaze. Set within opulent surroundings that recall Gatsby–era decadence, Huitema’s women bear the markers of high society themselves, dressed in elegant gowns and adorned with pearl necklaces or jewel-studded headdresses. Moving through film-noir settings with poise and a quietly calculating air, these femme fatales seem either to lure their audience into a seductive ruse or to deploy their own cunning to evade danger. In Sleeper Car, for example, a woman fitted in a backless evening gown tilts her head slyly over her right shoulder in a relaxed pose while her right hand appears braced and ready to strike. As rain streaks across the coach’s windows and the narrow aisle stretches into an uncertain depth, a moment of cinematic suspense emerges, evoking the apex of a psychological thriller. In this way, Huitema constructs a world of heightened atmosphere and theatrical tension that opens onto the broader visual traditions and painterly languages informing her work.

Huitema’s paintings draw on a range of art-historical and visual references while maintaining a distinct internal coherence. The attenuated proportions and stylized poses of her figures recall traditions of early twentieth-century fashion illustration and Art Deco design, where gesture and embellishment echo the streamlined finesse of illustrators such as Erté and the theatrical poise found in interwar couture and stage design. Her compressed spaces also suggest affinities with aspects of Symbolist and Surrealist painting, in which shallow interiors and phantasmagoric backdrops function less as coherent environments than as psychological realms shaped by subconscious experience. Rather than aligning with a single historical framework, Huitema synthesizes these influences into a contemporary visual language that moves fluidly between illustration, painting, and cinematic staging. Working outside formal academic training, she has developed this vocabulary through sustained studio practice and close observation, resulting in a body of work that situates itself in dialogue with art history while remaining grounded in a self-directed approach to image making. In this context, Prussian Blue operates not only as a chromatic throughline but also as a conceptual one, binding together Huitema’s historical references and recurring motifs of protection and threat in constant tension.

#9168. Molly Bounds "The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins" @ Mrs Gallery, Maspeth, NY

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ New York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her new series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

There are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less important; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

A Brighton studio of Northerners, a 25-hour RPG and a free game engine. It’s set in 2002, so nobody has a smartphone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Plenty of Pokémon imitators have come along over the years, with the most brazen in recent years being Palworld. But look at 2023's Cassette Beasts, and you see how a creature-collecting game can offer a unique twist without following the same mascot-based formula. For one, it wasn't really about catching creatures but recording and then transforming into them yourself. Speaking to Bytten Studio's co-founder, art and game director Jay Bayliss, it had been important very early on to consider how Cassette Beasts would distinguish itself.

"We had the idea of fusion as a central mechanic, which Pokemon can't tap into because Pikachu is a mascot that you can't dilute by merging it with a thousand other beasts to get new beasts," he explains. "We also thought about focusing on the human characters, so maybe the beasts could be a reflection of the human characters, which led to the idea of transforming into them."

It also helped that Cassette Beasts aimed itself at a slightly older audience compared to every Pokemon game always having you start out as yet another schoolkid, though its British humour and sensibilities also stood out, which is something the Brighton-based studio is leaning even more directly on with its upcoming sequel.

Cassette Beasts 2002 is set in London (as well as its alternate world of Nodnol), but it aims not to give the tourist version of the capital, but a quieter Zone 6 suburb version of it, with the town of Elmwich.

"We don't lean into a certain Paddington-esque twee Britishism about it," Bayliss explains. "Crucially, we're Northerners living down South in Brighton; we don't really play with that twee Britishness. We enjoy portraying quite a mundane, crappy version of suburban English life. We're so bored of the Harry Potter-esque upper middle-class boarding school fantasy take on it. I think this version's more fun."

As the title's palindrome suggests, Cassette Beasts 2002 is also set in 2002. That appeals to me personally, much like one of my favourite indie games released earlier this year, Perfect Tides: Station to Station, because it taps into my formative teen years. "The early 2000s also mark this crossing point between the analogue and digital age," Bayliss explains. "The internet exists, but you don't have smartphones. People do have mobile phones in the game, but we haven't got the Panopticon of social media. For artists younger than me, they reflect on this ethereal time they just missed out on, just before we had the baggage of the modern world overwhelming you."

It was also important to reflect the era's aesthetic and fashion. "Skewing male, game developers often don't appreciate fashion, but if you go on TikTok and social media, people are very interested in noughties fashion," Bayliss explains. "There's a lot of interest in exploring that time that we don't discount, and that's reflected in the fashion sensibilities of the characters and the character designs themselves as well."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Perhaps a major visual shift with this sequel is a more 3D one. Well, it's a case of perspective, literally. The original Cassette Beasts, while presented in the traditional top-down perspective of classic Pokemon and other 8- and 16-bit RPGs, was actually made in a 3D engine, albeit with environments given pixelated textures to match its 2D character sprites. In Cassette Beasts 2002, the camera drops down so things are presented as a third-person 3D game, except its characters are still pixel-art sprites presented with a billboarding technique.

"We were like, what if we can design this game with higher resolution sprites, with eight directions so when you pan the camera around, it feels less awkward?" Bayliss explains. "From a technical point of view, you have to rethink how you're designing worlds, but suddenly the perspective and scale you have in these worlds is very different. If you took the first game and dropped the camera down, it would probably feel very small, so it changes how we sculpt and design the world."

Cassette Beasts 2002 is also developed with the open-source Godot engine, which more indies are turning to. Although Bayliss recalls the challenges of porting the game's predecessor, which was developed with Godot 3, the latest iteration, Godot 4, that the studio is using has greatly improved features, including porting and performance, that make it a more viable alternative to Unity.

"If you sign up to Unity, you're kind of on the hook for any changes that Unity makes, whereas with an open-source engine, if you don't like changes, you can change the engine," Bayliss explains. "I think the flexibility of Godot is what allows a team of two full-time developers to make a big 25-hour RPG. It's just a very uncomplicated engine - you make stuff, you put it in, it's in the game. If there's anything that you need to fix, you don't have to submit a bug report to the back-end team and hope they fix it in the next two years; you just go in and fix it yourself."

Cassette Beasts 2002 is releasing in March 2027 for PC, Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, and Nintendo Switch 2. You can wishlist it now on Steam.

#9166. ICA Miami selects architect to renovate recently acquired building

Rendering of ICA Miami’s new building Courtesy Gensler

The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami (ICA Miami) has appointed the global architecture firm Gensler to renovate a 30,000-sq.-ft building the museum acquired in 2024, doubling its exhibition and public-programming space.

Steps away from its current venue in Miami’s Design District, the new wing is scheduled to open in late 2027—as the museum marks its tenth anniversary at its current location. Focused on expanding the free museum’s community outreach, the project will transform the ICA into a multi-site complex and house the first permanent display of its collection.

The museum’s new building formerly housed the De la Cruz Collection, a private museum that closed after the 2024 death of its co-founder Rosa de la Cruz. Since its $25m acquisition later that year, the site has mainly hosted the ICA’s educational programmes. It will close once construction begins. The renovation is part of a $40m capital campaign, supported entirely by private funds.

The new design will adapt the existing structure. “The building was developed to house a contemporary art collection,” Alex Gartenfeld, the ICA’s director and chief curator, tells The Art Newspaper. “But with the spaces we are constructing, we intend to enhance the museum’s story-driven narrative approach to the collection and exhibitions.”

Rendering of ICA Miami’s new building Courtesy Gensler

Eight new galleries will occupy the building’s first and second floors. Among them will be the museum’s first dedicated spaces for its growing permanent collection of more than 2,000 works.

“The programme between the two buildings is blended, but we will now have two full floors dedicated to our permanent collection,” Gartenfeld says. “Around every six months, we will refresh the collection display to reflect the collection’s emphasis and recent acquisitions.”

The entire third floor will be dedicated to public programming, including talks, symposia, lectures and performances. “Beyond adding galleries, this renovation will strengthen the ICA’s ability to support artists, expand learning and create a platform for exchange and belonging in one of the world’s most dynamic cultural cities,” says Bevin Savage Yamazaki, Gensler’s global culture and museums leader.

A reimagined façade with transparent components is key to the design. Gartenfeld says the façade aims to provide a connection between street-level traffic and the museum itself.

The renovations focus on visitor experience and accessibility as well. The lobby will be redesigned. And reconfigured outdoor areas will include social spaces, a sculpture deck and an expanded café. “We are aiming to create a more collective experience,” Gartenfeld says.

The museum expanded its exhibition space and reorganised its permanent collection for the first time in almost 100 years—with a special focus on Native American art

#9165. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.
